messages.content: I need a design for live firmware updates on an embedded controller. The control loop must keep meeting its 1 ms deadlines throughout an uninterrupted update, and actuator commands cannot be duplicated or skipped. Firmware updates may change the state schema: incompatible migrations must be rejected atomically, and after any update-time reset the controller must recover a compatible firmware-state pair. How should I frame the design?

Frame it around three invariants rather than around the mechanics of loading firmware. During uninterrupted operation, each 1 ms control deadline remains satisfied. Each control interval has exactly one actuator-command owner, so a handoff cannot produce either a duplicate or a missing command. Finally, the firmware selected for execution and the state selected with it must form a compatible pair, including after a reset at any point in the update.

A possible design separates preparation from promotion: keep the current firmware-state pair responsible for control while a candidate firmware-state pair is prepared and checked. Promote the candidate only at a defined control boundary, after migration compatibility and recovery conditions are established. That is a design pattern to evaluate, not an assumption that the controller already has the resources to implement it.
Does meeting the 1 ms deadline mean the update can briefly stop control and catch up afterward?

No. For an uninterrupted update, a later burst does not repair a missed 1 ms deadline. Preparation, migration, validation, and the final handoff must be arranged so that their interference with the control path stays within the deadline on every affected interval. The handoff itself must also have a bounded control-path cost; a correct state migration would not compensate for a control interval that ran late.
What does one actuator-command owner mean if the old and new firmware are both present during the update?

Presence need not imply authority to command actuators. Conceptually, associate each control interval with one owner and one command opportunity. The current firmware remains the owner until the handoff boundary; the candidate becomes the owner only for intervals assigned to it after that boundary. There must not be an interval both can command, nor an interval neither commands.

An interval identifier or equivalent ownership rule could help enforce this, but its form depends on the controller and actuator interface. The important property is exactly one effective command per required interval, not merely that both firmware versions calculate plausible outputs.
If both versions would send the same actuator value, would sending it twice still be a problem?

Yes. The requirement concerns duplicated commands, not only whether their values differ. Two submissions of an identical value can still be two commands. Likewise, retaining a previous output is not automatically proof that the required command for the next interval was issued. The design needs to account for command occurrences at the handoff, separately from the numerical values being commanded.
The schema change is the part that worries me. Control state may still be changing while the candidate state is being prepared.

That makes consistency at the boundary essential. A migrated state prepared from an earlier view cannot simply be installed if it no longer represents the active control state at handoff. The design needs a way to obtain a coherent state for promotion—whether by capturing state at a suitable boundary or by accounting for changes that occurred during preparation—and it must establish that the candidate firmware can interpret that resulting state.

The particular transfer mechanism cannot be chosen from the requirements alone. Whichever mechanism is used must fit the 1 ms deadline and must not grant the candidate actuator ownership before its state is ready.
What exactly should atomic rejection of an incompatible migration protect?

It should protect the active firmware-state pair and actuator ownership from a partial transition. If compatibility checks fail, the candidate must not become the controlling firmware, its migrated state must not replace the active state, and the update must not leave behind a handoff in which actuator commands are duplicated or skipped. From the control path's perspective, an incompatible candidate is rejected as a unit rather than being partly applied.

Compatibility is more than whether a representation can be decoded. The migrated state must meet the conditions the candidate firmware requires to continue control correctly. Those conditions have to be specified for the actual schemas; they cannot be inferred merely from matching field names.
So rejection should not require trying the candidate in control and then undoing its actuator commands?

Right. A rejected migration should not require reversing commands that have already reached actuators. Compatibility and readiness need to be established before the candidate receives command authority. If a candidate is rejected, the continuing control path should remain the compatible pair that was already in charge. This keeps rejection atomic with respect to externally visible control, rather than treating an attempted rollout and rollback as harmless.
How does the reset requirement change that picture?

It adds a persistent pairing invariant. At every point where an update-time reset might occur, recovery must be able to choose firmware together with state that it can interpret. An incomplete candidate must not be mistaken for a committed pair, and committing a new firmware selection without its compatible state—or the reverse—would violate the requirement.

Conceptually, preparation should leave a recoverable compatible pair available; promotion should make the new pair recoverably selectable only when both sides and the information needed to select them are ready. The exact persistence mechanism depends on the available storage and its reset behavior.
Suppose the reset happens right in the middle of making the new pair current. What must recovery do?

It must resolve that interrupted transition to a compatible pair, not combine whichever firmware and state happen to be easiest to read. A recoverable commit boundary needs an unambiguous way to distinguish an incomplete candidate from a committed pair. If the new pair was not made recoverably committed, recovery can select the retained compatible pair; if it was, recovery can select the new compatible pair. The design must cover a reset at every intermediate point, including the boundary itself.

That describes the required behavior, not a claim that any particular write sequence or storage device already provides it. The persistence guarantees and failure assumptions would need to be checked before choosing a concrete commit method.
Does ‘after any update-time reset’ also require uninterrupted 1 ms control across the reset?

The two clauses should be kept distinct. The 1 ms deadline and no-duplicate-or-skipped-command requirement applies throughout uninterrupted updates. A reset interrupts execution; the stated reset requirement is that recovery yields a compatible firmware-state pair. It does not, by itself, establish that control deadlines were met while the controller was reset.

Similarly, command delivery across a reset would need its own definition and supporting mechanism if that were required. It should not be silently claimed as part of compatible-pair recovery.
Would isolating update work from the control loop be enough to establish the timing guarantee?

Isolation helps, but it is not sufficient as a statement on its own. The timing argument must include any update work that can still affect a control interval: interference during preparation, state capture or synchronization, compatibility checks that touch live state, the handoff, and any persistence operation that blocks control. Each uninterrupted interval must retain enough time to meet its 1 ms deadline.

Without the controller's execution and storage characteristics, no numerical budget beyond the stated 1 ms deadline can responsibly be claimed. The design should identify what must be bounded, then verify those bounds on the intended system.
Can the candidate wait if its state is valid but the handoff cannot yet fit within a control interval?

Yes, conceptually: readiness to migrate and readiness to hand off are separate conditions. Until a handoff can preserve the deadline and single-command-owner rules, the current compatible pair should remain in control. The requirement is to maintain deadlines throughout an uninterrupted update; it does not state a maximum time by which an update must finish. Waiting is preferable to forcing a transition that creates a late, duplicate, or skipped command.
How would you turn all of this into checks for a proposed implementation?

Check three properties together. For timing, account for every control interval during preparation and handoff against the 1 ms deadline, including worst-case interference. For actuator consistency, trace ownership and effective command issuance across the boundary: every required interval has one command, with neither duplicates nor gaps. For migration and recovery, exercise incompatible candidates and resets at every meaningful update point, checking that rejection has no partial control effect and that recovery always selects a compatible firmware-state pair.

Those are acceptance criteria for a design, not results already demonstrated. A concrete implementation would also need its compatibility rules, command-interface semantics, and reset-persistence guarantees defined before the checks could be completed.

Could we make the design more concrete by keeping the 1-ms scheduler and actuator driver resident, validating migrations in shadow state, atomically switching between A/B firmware-state pairs, and sequence-fencing actuator commands?

Yes—that is a coherent proposal for the stated requirements. The resident 1-ms scheduler and actuator driver would remain outside the firmware-state pair being switched. A candidate pair could be prepared and its shadow migration validated without giving it actuator authority. At a defined control boundary, the design would switch the selected firmware and its corresponding state together. Sequence fencing at the command path would distinguish commands belonging to the authorized interval and owner from duplicates or stale submissions.

Each part has a different job. Keeping scheduling resident supports continuity of control timing; shadow validation supports atomic rejection of incompatible migrations; switching A/B pairs together supports firmware-state compatibility; and command fencing supports exactly-once actuator-command behavior. The proposal still needs a timing and recovery argument—it is not a guarantee merely because these components are named.
What does ‘resident’ mean here? Is the scheduler part of the firmware being exchanged?

In this proposal, ‘resident’ means the 1-ms scheduler and actuator driver continue operating across the firmware-state switch rather than being exchanged as part of the A/B pair at that handoff. That gives the control intervals and actuator-command path a stable point of coordination while the selected firmware-state pair changes.

It does not mean update activity can never interfere with them. The design must still show that preparation, validation, the switch, and any shared-resource contention leave every uninterrupted control interval within its 1 ms deadline.
Why keep the actuator driver resident as well as the scheduler?

The scheduler can define when control work belongs to an interval; the resident driver can provide one consistent enforcement point for commands across the switch. If command authority changed merely because two firmware versions were present, both might try to issue a command for the same interval, or neither might issue one. A driver that remains in place can apply the same ownership and sequence-fencing rule on both sides of the handoff.

That still requires defining what counts as an effective actuator command. Rejecting a duplicate must not inadvertently reject the sole command for an interval, and a correctly timed scheduler invocation must not be mistaken for proof that a command actually reached the actuator path.
Walk me through what is supposed to happen to state before the A/B switch.

The candidate firmware-state pair stays separate from the pair currently responsible for control. Its state is prepared as a shadow migration, then checked for compatibility with the candidate firmware before the pair can be selected. ‘Shadow’ matters because a failed check can reject the candidate without partly replacing the active state or transferring actuator authority.

The check must also address consistency with state that may change during preparation. A shadow copy that was valid when created is not necessarily the right state for the eventual handoff. The proposed switch is safe only if the state selected with the candidate is coherent at that boundary and compatible with that firmware.
Does A/B mean switching firmware first and then switching state?

No. The proposed unit of selection is a firmware-state pair, not an independently chosen firmware version followed by a separately chosen state. ‘Atomically switch’ means the control path must not observe an intermediate combination in which the candidate firmware runs with incompatible state or the previous firmware is paired with candidate-only state.

The same pairing principle matters for recovery after an update-time reset. A/B describes the availability of alternative pairs; by itself, it does not specify how selection survives a reset. That part needs a recoverable, unambiguous commit rule for the pair.
Can a shadow migration be considered validated just because its data can be decoded?

No. Decoding establishes only that a representation can be read. Validation must establish that the migrated state is compatible with the candidate firmware’s expectations for continuing control. It must also establish that the state to be selected reflects a coherent handoff state, rather than an earlier snapshot that has become inconsistent while the active pair continued running.

The proposal does not specify particular schema fields or migration rules, so those checks cannot be reduced to a named field-by-field test here. If validation fails, the candidate pair must not be partially selected.
Then what is the sequence fence doing that the atomic pair switch does not do?

The pair switch addresses which firmware and state are selected together. The sequence fence addresses which actuator-command submission is authorized for a control interval. Even with an atomic pair selection, work begun near the boundary could attempt to submit a command on the wrong side of it. The driver needs to distinguish the authorized command from an old, repeated, or otherwise out-of-turn submission.

Fencing is not just duplicate suppression. The design must also ensure that every required interval has an authorized producer able to deliver its command. A fence that prevents two commands but leaves an interval with zero would fail the no-skipped-commands requirement.
Is it accurate to say that the old pair owns the interval before the switch and the new pair owns the interval after it?

That captures the intended boundary, provided ‘before’ and ‘after’ are defined by control intervals rather than by an ambiguous instant during execution. Each interval must have exactly one assigned command owner. A command associated with an earlier interval must not become a second command for a later one, and a command from the candidate must not be accepted before its assigned interval.

The proposal does not prescribe the representation of a sequence or the exact instant at which ownership changes. Those details have to make the pair switch and the driver’s fence agree on the same interval boundary.
If shadow validation fails, do we have to perform an A/B switch and then switch back?

No. Validation of the shadow migration is a condition for selecting the candidate pair. If it is incompatible, rejection should leave the current firmware-state pair and its command authority in place. That is the atomic-rejection aspect: an incompatible candidate does not become partly active and does not require reversing actuator commands already sent under it.

The resident scheduler still has to meet each 1 ms deadline during the attempted update and rejection. A failed migration is not permission to pause or catch up later.
What if validation passes but performing the switch would overrun the next deadline?

Passing migration validation is necessary but not sufficient for promotion. The switch also has to fit the uninterrupted-update timing requirement, including any effect on the resident scheduler and driver. If a handoff cannot be performed while meeting the 1 ms deadline and preserving one command per interval, it should not occur at that boundary.

The proposal does not supply execution times or a deadline budget for the switch, so it cannot establish in advance that every possible handoff will fit. That must be shown for the intended controller.
How should I think about a reset during shadow preparation versus a reset during the atomic switch?

In either case, recovery must select a compatible firmware-state pair. During shadow preparation, an incomplete candidate must not be selected as though it were ready. Around the switch, recovery must be able to determine which complete pair is recoverably selected without assembling firmware from one pair and state from the other.

Calling the switch atomic describes the required observable result; it does not by itself prove reset safety. The design needs persistence and selection behavior that remains unambiguous if a reset occurs at any update-time point, including during the transition.
Would the sequence fence alone tell recovery which A/B pair to load?

Not necessarily. The fence governs actuator-command authorization; recovery needs to identify a compatible firmware-state pair. Those are related at the handoff, but they are distinct questions. A command sequence should not be treated as proof that both firmware and state were recoverably committed unless the design explicitly establishes that relationship.

The recovery argument must stand on the pair-selection guarantees. The command argument must separately show that an uninterrupted switch neither duplicates nor skips actuator commands.
Can you state the proposal without implying it has already been verified?

Propose keeping the 1-ms scheduler and actuator driver resident while preparing an updated firmware-state pair separately. Validate its shadow state migration before selection. If validation succeeds and the handoff can meet the 1 ms control deadline, atomically select the candidate A/B firmware-state pair at a control boundary. Use sequence fencing in the resident actuator-command path so that each required interval has one authorized command, with no duplicates or skips. If migration is incompatible, reject the candidate without partially changing the active pair. Make pair selection recoverable so any update-time reset leads to a compatible firmware-state pair.

That states the intended architecture and obligations. Whether a particular implementation satisfies them remains to be demonstrated.
How can the resident scheduler switch firmware-state pairs on a tick boundary without replaying or skipping an actuator sequence?

Treat the tick boundary as a transfer of ownership of the *next* actuator sequence, not as an instruction to run a tick again. The resident scheduler should have one progression of control ticks. For a handoff between ticks, the old firmware-state pair owns the last tick before the boundary, and the new pair owns the first tick after it. The resident actuator driver applies the same sequence rule on both sides: it accepts the authorized command for a tick once, and does not accept another command as a replay of that tick.

That describes the invariant the switch must implement; it does not assume a particular counter representation or that the handoff is already proven to fit the 1 ms deadline.
Can you illustrate the boundary without depending on a specific actuator protocol?

Call the last tick assigned to the old pair tick N and the first assigned to the new pair tick N+1. The old pair may supply the command for N, but not for N+1. The new pair may supply the command for N+1, but must not supply another command for N. The scheduler advances from N to N+1 once, while the driver checks each submission against the tick and pair authorized to produce it.

The letters and numbers are only an illustration. The substantive requirement is that changing the selected pair neither repeats the sequence position already served nor advances past one that still needs its command.
Why isn't switching the firmware and state together sufficient?

An atomic pair switch prevents the control path from selecting firmware with the wrong state. It does not, on its own, settle what happens to command work near the boundary. Work initiated under the old pair might still reach the driver after selection changes, or the new pair might attempt to command a tick that the old pair has already served. Conversely, if each side assumes the other is responsible for the boundary tick, neither may provide its command.

The scheduler's tick assignment and the driver's sequence fence must therefore agree with the pair-selection boundary. Pair atomicity protects state compatibility; sequence ownership protects actuator-command continuity.
Should the switch happen before or after the old pair sends its command?

It needs to be specified relative to *completion of the tick being handed off*, not merely described as ‘during a tick.’ One understandable boundary is: the old pair remains responsible for a designated final tick and its command; only subsequent ticks belong to the new pair. The switch must not reassign that final tick after its command is accepted, and must not leave the following tick without an owner.

The exact placement depends on how the controller defines a completed command and a tick boundary. Whichever placement is chosen, the ownership rule must cover any submission still in flight and must meet the 1 ms timing constraint.
What does sequence-fencing an in-flight old command mean in this setting?

It means its origin and assigned tick remain relevant even if it arrives at the driver after the selected pair has changed. An old command for a tick already served cannot become another effective command for that tick. An old command must not be misinterpreted as the new pair's command for a subsequent tick either. The driver has to evaluate it under the agreed ownership and sequence rule rather than simply accepting it because it arrived.

But a fence must not discard the *only* required command for a tick. The switch cannot claim correctness from duplicate suppression alone; it must also account for delivery of each assigned tick's command.
Does the new pair start its actuator sequence at the beginning because it is new firmware?

No. Firmware replacement must not reset the actuator-command progression for an uninterrupted update. The new pair takes the next tick assigned by the resident scheduler, with the driver continuing to enforce one effective command per required tick. A pair-local notion of starting fresh would be unsafe if it caused a previously served tick to be commanded again.

That does not prescribe where a sequence identifier is stored or how it is encoded. The necessary property is a single, unambiguous progression across the pair change.
What if the new pair is ready, but a command from the old pair hasn't finished passing through the driver?

Readiness of the new firmware-state pair is not enough to resolve that command's status. The handoff rule must say whether the old pair's last assigned tick has been served and how any outstanding submission is handled before the next pair can command its assigned tick. It cannot count a submission twice, silently abandon the only submission for a required tick, or allow the outstanding old work to impersonate new work.

This is why the switch boundary should be stated in terms of tick ownership and effective commands, not just when a pointer to the selected pair changes. The handling of outstanding work also has to remain within the control deadline.
Could the scheduler dispatch the boundary tick to both pairs and let the driver pick one?

That would make the no-duplicate requirement depend on arbitration between two would-be owners, and it would complicate the question of which state produced the command. A cleaner statement of the proposed handoff is that each tick has one assigned pair before execution, and the driver rejects submissions inconsistent with that assignment. The driver is then a fence enforcing ownership, not a substitute for deciding ownership.

If an implementation did evaluate both pairs for some reason, it would still have to demonstrate that only the designated pair produces the effective command and that the extra work does not endanger the 1 ms deadline. Such concurrent evaluation is not required by the question.
Would it work to skip the boundary tick and resume at the next one if the switch takes too long?

No. That would skip a required actuator command, and a later command does not retroactively fill the gap. If a switch cannot fit at a proposed boundary while preserving the 1 ms deadline and the command for each tick, it should not take ownership away from the current pair at that boundary. The switch must be scheduled only at a boundary where its timing and command obligations can be satisfied.
Is a monotonically progressing tick label enough to prove no commands were skipped?

Not by itself. Labels can progress even if no effective command was issued for one of them. The argument needs two parts: ticks progress without replay, and each tick requiring an actuator command has exactly one effective command accepted under its assigned owner. Likewise, seeing one submission per label is insufficient if a submission was rejected or never became an effective actuator command.

The meaning of ‘accepted’ or ‘effective’ needs to match the actual actuator interface; the tick label is a way to reason about the sequence, not a replacement for that observation.
How do we tell whether the switch has actually preserved both properties?

Trace the boundary across consecutive ticks. For each one, identify the selected firmware-state pair, its assigned command ownership, and the command the resident driver actually accepts. The trace should show exactly one effective command for the old pair's last assigned tick and exactly one for the new pair's first assigned tick, with no tick repeated or omitted. Include cases where a submission reaches the driver close to the boundary, since those are where an ownership mistake might appear.

Separately, check the elapsed control-path work for those ticks against the 1 ms deadline. A clean command trace does not prove timing, and meeting the deadline does not prove that the actuator sequence was neither replayed nor skipped.
So what is the shortest rule I could give an implementer for the handoff?

Give every tick exactly one firmware-state-pair owner before it can issue an actuator command; move ownership only between ticks; keep the scheduler's tick progression continuous; and have the resident driver accept at most the authorized command for each tick. Then verify that the rule delivers *exactly one* effective command for every required tick, including the two adjacent to the switch, while both still meet their 1 ms deadlines. The exact handoff and fencing mechanisms remain implementation choices subject to those checks.

My hypothesis is that a tick-boundary pointer swap, together with a resident monotonic command counter, can keep dispatch below 1 ms with zero duplicated or missing actuator commands. Does that answer the handoff question?

It is a plausible answer, but it is a hypothesis rather than an established timing or command-delivery result. The pointer swap would make the selected firmware-state pair change at a tick boundary, while the resident counter would provide a continuous command sequence across that change. The claim to demonstrate is that dispatch stays below 1 ms and that the actual actuator-command sequence has neither duplicates nor gaps.

The two mechanisms address different parts of the handoff. A tick-boundary swap identifies which pair is selected for each tick; a resident counter gives command progression a reference that does not restart with the selected pair. Neither property, stated alone, proves that every required command becomes effective exactly once.
Why emphasize that the counter is resident?

Because the hypothesis relies on command progression continuing across the firmware-state-pair switch. If each pair began its own count, the same sequence position could appear on both sides of the boundary, or the first position expected after the switch could be unclear. A resident monotonic counter is intended to give both sides one continuous reference.

‘Monotonic’ says the counter moves forward; it does not say when it moves forward or what event a count represents. Those meanings must be defined before the counter can support a claim of zero duplicates or gaps.
Can you put the hypothesis in terms of the two ticks around the swap?

Using illustrative ticks N and N+1, the current firmware-state pair would be selected for N, and the candidate pair would be selected for N+1 after the tick-boundary pointer swap. The resident command counter would continue its progression across those ticks rather than starting again for the candidate. The desired observation is one effective actuator command for N and one for N+1, with no second command for either and no missing command between them.

That illustration expresses the hypothesis; it does not establish that the pointer swap, counter behavior, or dispatch time actually has those properties on a particular controller.
If the pointer changes exactly at the boundary, doesn't that already settle ownership?

It can settle which pair *should* own each tick, provided the scheduler and command path agree on what that boundary means. The difficult part is ensuring that a submission associated with the old pair cannot be mistaken for a new-tick command merely because it arrives after the pointer changes, and that the new pair cannot replay a command for the previous tick.

Thus the pointer swap is a proposed ownership boundary, not by itself a complete account of command acceptance. The resident counter has to be interpreted consistently with that boundary.
Is the claim really about a pointer swap, or about switching firmware and state as a pair?

The pointer swap is the proposed mechanism for selecting the firmware-state pair at the tick boundary. Its target must represent a compatible pair, not an independently changed firmware selection and state selection. Otherwise, an apparently clean tick boundary could still expose firmware to state it cannot interpret.

The command-counter part of the hypothesis does not replace that pairing requirement. It concerns the actuator sequence, while the pair selection concerns what code and state produce the command.
Suppose the counter increases for N and N+1. Would that prove there was no gap?

No. A counter can advance even if a command for one of those ticks never becomes an effective actuator command. To support the no-gap claim, each required counter position must correspond to a command that the actuator path actually accepts under the intended ownership rule. Similarly, no-duplicate behavior requires excluding a second effective command for the same position; distinct counter values on two attempted submissions would not automatically rule out an unintended extra command.

The hypothesis therefore needs a precise relationship between the resident counter, tick assignment, and effective command delivery. Merely observing increasing numbers would be weaker than observing zero duplicates or gaps.
Could the counter itself prevent a late command from the old pair from being replayed?

It could serve as the basis for fencing such a submission if the command path checks which sequence position and pair are authorized. A late old-pair submission must not become a second effective command for a position already served, nor be relabeled as the new pair's command for the next position. But a monotonic counter alone is only state; preventing replay depends on how the driver uses it when accepting commands.

That is a condition on the hypothesis, not an assertion that a specific counter-checking implementation has already been chosen or verified.
What if the driver refuses the late old command? Does that establish the no-gap part?

Only if that late submission was not the sole required command for its assigned tick. Refusing an unauthorized duplicate supports the no-duplicate part; refusing the only command for a required tick would create a gap. At the boundary, the reasoning must identify both the final command belonging to the old pair and the first belonging to the new pair, then show that each becomes effective once.

This is why ‘zero duplicates or gaps’ is a stronger claim than ‘the counter is monotonic’ or ‘the driver rejects stale work.’
How should I read the phrase ‘dispatch below 1 ms’ in the hypothesis?

Read it as a timing claim that remains to be demonstrated for the handoff, including the costs that affect dispatch at the tick boundary. A pointer swap sounds small, but its name does not establish the time taken by selection, synchronization with command ownership, or any relevant interference. The proposed mechanism must keep dispatch below 1 ms under the conditions in which the update is performed.

Also distinguish dispatch time from the broader control deadline: if ‘dispatch’ measures only part of the control path, a result below 1 ms for that part would not alone prove that the entire required 1 ms control deadline is met. The hypothesis should state clearly what is being timed.
Could a switch meet the timing claim but still fail the command claim?

Yes. Dispatch might complete below 1 ms while the boundary tick produces two effective commands, or while neither pair produces one for a required sequence position. Timing and actuator-sequence continuity are independent checks. The hypothesis asserts both: dispatch below 1 ms *and* zero duplicates or gaps. Evidence for one should not be taken as evidence for the other.
And could the sequence look perfect while the deadline is missed?

Yes. Exactly one effective command per required tick would not establish that the command was dispatched in time. A late but nonduplicated command still fails the real-time requirement. The proposed pointer swap and counter have to be evaluated against both the 1 ms timing bound and the command-sequence condition, particularly on the ticks adjacent to the swap.
Does ‘tick-boundary’ imply the current pair has finished all work when the pointer changes?

Not automatically. It names where ownership is intended to change, but the design still has to account for work associated with the previous tick that may reach the command path near that boundary. A valid interpretation of the swap cannot turn such work into a replay, and it cannot discard a command that the previous tick still requires.

The hypothesis is strongest when ‘tick boundary’ is defined in terms of completed command obligations and ownership of the next tick, rather than only the instant at which a pointer is modified.
Does the hypothesis say anything about an incompatible shadow migration?

It addresses the tick-boundary handoff, not the full migration decision. Within the proposed update design, an incompatible migration must be rejected before the candidate firmware-state pair is selected. A fast pointer swap and a continuous counter would not make an incompatible pair safe to activate. For this hypothesis, the pair considered for a switch must already satisfy the separate compatibility condition.
What about an update-time reset? Would a resident command counter prove recoverability?

No. The counter is proposed to maintain command progression during an uninterrupted handoff. Recovering a compatible firmware-state pair after any update-time reset is a separate obligation. Neither a tick-boundary pointer swap nor a monotonic counter, by itself, establishes which complete pair recovery will select.

The hypothesis should therefore not be stretched into a claim that reset recovery has been solved. It is focused on dispatch time and absence of actuator-sequence duplicates or gaps across an uninterrupted switch.
What would be the most careful way to state the hypothesis for review?

‘We hypothesize that selecting a compatible firmware-state pair with a tick-boundary pointer swap, while maintaining a resident monotonic command counter across the switch, can keep dispatch below 1 ms and yield zero duplicated or missing effective actuator commands. This requires a shared definition of tick ownership and command acceptance at the boundary and remains to be demonstrated.’

That wording retains the specific mechanism and numerical claim without presenting the expected outcome as an observed result.
So the counter is evidence only if it tracks the sequence the driver actually enforces?

Exactly. It must have a defined relationship to the driver's effective actuator-command sequence and to the scheduler's assignment of ticks. Otherwise, a monotonic count could coexist with a duplicate, a gap, or a late command. The pointer swap and counter form a testable explanation for how the boundary might work; the claimed below-1-ms dispatch and zero duplicates or gaps are still outcomes to establish.
To check the handoff, I plan to profile 10,000 tick-boundary swaps under peak load. For each swap, I want to verify sub-1-ms dispatch and contiguous resident-issued actuator sequence IDs.

That is a focused plan for examining the tick-boundary handoff. It tests two distinct observations across 10,000 swaps under peak load: whether dispatch stays below 1 ms, and whether the sequence IDs issued by the resident command path continue contiguously across each switch. Neither observation should be treated as a result before the profiling and verification are done.

The boundaries matter most. For each swap, the sequence check needs to include the last ID issued before the switch and the first issued after it, not just IDs well away from the handoff.
Should I report average dispatch time over the 10,000 swaps?

An average could provide context, but it would not verify sub-1-ms dispatch for the handoff. A few swaps at or above 1 ms could be hidden by a lower average. If the planned claim is that dispatch stays below 1 ms, examine each measured swap, including the slowest one, rather than relying only on an aggregate.

Also state what the measurement calls ‘dispatch.’ A sub-1-ms measurement of one part of the control path should not silently become a claim that the entire 1 ms control deadline was met.
Why emphasize peak load instead of just repeating the swap 10,000 times?

The intended test is 10,000 tick-boundary swaps *under peak load*. The count gives repeated opportunities to observe the handoff; the load condition addresses whether dispatch and sequence continuity hold when competing work is at its intended peak. Repeating swaps under an easier condition would not be the same plan.

‘Peak load’ needs a definition for the controller being assessed, but this plan does not specify its workload or numerical characteristics. Those should not be assumed from the phrase alone.
What would count as a contiguous resident-issued actuator sequence across one swap?

The resident-issued IDs immediately across the boundary should follow the same progression as IDs away from it: the first ID issued after the switch is the successor of the last one issued before it, with no repeated or omitted position. Looking across the full trace for the swap also matters; checking only those two IDs might overlook another issuance nearby.

This is a check on the resident-issued sequence IDs. Its meaning depends on observing issuance consistently on both sides of the boundary.
If the first ID after a swap is the right successor, can I say there was no replay?

You can say that particular comparison shows no repeated or skipped *ID at that point in the observed issuance sequence*. It would not, by itself, prove that an actuator command was never replayed. For example, a duplicate effective command might carry the same ID, or a trace that records each ID only once might conceal repeated issuance.
