I have a revised hypothesis for cutover: prewarm the candidate code and state, give the latch interrupt priority over cutover, and swap only after acknowledgment. The intended result is that each 1-ms tick latches once. How should I reason about it?

Treat it as an ordering hypothesis, not a demonstrated result. Prewarming the candidate code and state is intended to reduce work that would otherwise compete with a tick at cutover. Prioritizing the latch interrupt means cutover must yield when the tick’s latch operation needs attention. Swapping after acknowledgment puts the pair change on the far side of an identified latch event rather than allowing the change to overlap it.

The outcome to establish is still precise: each 1-ms tick completes its required latch once, without a repeat or an omission, while its deadline is met. Naming those three measures does not yet show that their timing and synchronization achieve that outcome.
What exactly should ‘prewarm’ mean here? Does it mean the candidate may start commanding actuators?

No. In this hypothesis, prewarming means getting the candidate code and state ready for a potential cutover; it does not grant the candidate authority to issue actuator commands. The currently selected firmware-state pair remains responsible for its assigned tick until the cutover rule transfers ownership.

The proposal does not specify a particular prewarming mechanism. Whatever preparation is used must not itself interfere enough to miss a 1 ms deadline, and the candidate state still has to be compatible and coherent before selection.
Why prewarm both code and state rather than just code?

Because the selected unit is a firmware-state pair. Having code ready without the state it needs would not make the candidate ready to take over a tick; having state prepared without code ready would leave the other side of that pair unprepared. The hypothesis is that preparing both before the time-sensitive handoff limits what remains to be done at the boundary. It does not establish that either preparation is sufficient or that the final handoff has a particular duration.
What does giving the latch interrupt priority over cutover actually guarantee?

By itself, it states which work should take precedence when the latch interrupt and cutover contend. It does not guarantee the interrupt starts or completes before the 1 ms deadline, nor that its latch operation happens exactly once. Those properties require an account of when the interrupt can arrive, what cutover work can delay it, and what event confirms completion.

It is important not to turn ‘higher priority’ into ‘cannot be delayed at all.’ The timing claim needs to cover the actual path to the latch.
Is the acknowledgment meant to be acknowledgment of a command being issued, or of the actuator latch?

For the proposed ordering to address once-per-tick latching, the acknowledgment has to attest to the relevant latch obligation for that tick—not merely that a command ID was issued. The exact source and semantics of acknowledgment are not specified here. They need to be defined so that ‘swap after acknowledgment’ has an unambiguous relationship to completion of the tick’s latch.

An issuance acknowledgment alone could leave open whether the actuator latched, and a generic acknowledgment without a tick association could leave open which tick it covers.
Can you give a small boundary illustration?

Call the last tick assigned to the current pair N. Under the hypothesis, its latch operation gets priority over cutover. Once acknowledgment establishes that N’s required latch has completed, a cutover may select the prewarmed candidate pair for a subsequent tick. The candidate must not reinterpret that acknowledgment as permission to latch N again, and the switch must not leave the next tick without its own latch.

That is an illustration of the intended sequence, not proof that acknowledgment arrives early enough or that a particular implementation prevents all races.
If the latch interrupt arrives while the swap is being considered, should we finish the swap first because it is short?

That would not follow the proposed priority rule. The hypothesis gives the latch interrupt precedence over cutover, even if cutover is expected to be short. A short anticipated swap is not evidence that delaying the latch preserves its deadline. The implementation would have to make ‘latch before cutover when they contend’ meaningful at the relevant boundary.
Does ‘swap after acknowledgment’ mean I can change the selected pair at any later moment?

No. Acknowledgment supplies one necessary ordering condition; it does not erase the need for a well-defined tick boundary. The swap must still assign each tick to one firmware-state pair and must not split a tick’s command and latch obligations between pairs. If the appropriate boundary has passed, the design cannot simply swap at an arbitrary instant and call it safe because an earlier latch was acknowledged.
Could we swap right after the acknowledgment even if the next tick is already in progress?

The hypothesis does not justify changing ownership in the middle of a tick already assigned to a pair. ‘After acknowledgment’ should be read together with the tick-boundary handoff: finish the relevant latch obligation, then change pairs only at a boundary where the next tick’s ownership remains unambiguous. Otherwise the new pair and the current pair could disagree about who owes that tick’s latch.
What if acknowledgment does not arrive before the intended cutover boundary?

Then the stated precondition for that cutover has not been met. The hypothesis does not support swapping first and treating acknowledgment as something that can arrive afterward. Remaining with the current pair for that boundary is consistent with the proposed ordering, provided its continuing control also meets the deadline.

A late acknowledgment would itself require attention in the timing analysis. Deferring the swap prevents an unauthorized handoff; it does not retroactively make a late latch timely.
Is latching exactly once per tick the same as observing contiguous issued command IDs?

No. IDs describe a command sequence at its observation point. The hypothesis makes a claim about latch occurrences: each 1-ms tick latches once. A contiguous issued-ID sequence can coexist with a latch that repeats an output or fails to occur on time. To assess this hypothesis, the acknowledgment and observations must speak to the latch event, not only to the issuance of IDs.
If two consecutive ticks intentionally use the same actuator value, would that count as a repeated latch?

Not merely because the values match. ‘Each tick latches once’ concerns the occurrence and tick assignment of the latch operation, not whether successive commanded values are numerically different. Two ticks could each latch once with equal values; conversely, a repeated output within the handoff could be a problem even while issued IDs progress. The check needs to distinguish repeated values from repeated or missing latch obligations.
Does prioritizing the interrupt solve the once-per-tick part by itself?

No. Priority addresses contention for execution time. Exactly-once latching additionally requires that the latch obligation for a tick is neither performed twice nor treated as complete without being performed. The acknowledgment used to gate cutover must correspond to the right tick, and a pair change must not cause either pair to replay that tick’s latch or overlook the following one. Those are conditions the hypothesis proposes to satisfy, not consequences of priority alone.
Could acknowledgment be left over from an earlier tick and accidentally authorize the swap?

That is a logical ambiguity the cutover rule has to exclude. ‘After acknowledgment’ must mean acknowledgment of the latch obligation relevant to the proposed boundary, not just the presence of some earlier acknowledgment. The hypothesis does not specify how that association is represented, but without it the ordering claim would not identify which tick is complete.
How should I separate the timing claim from the latch-count claim?

Ask two questions for each tick affected by cutover. First, did its latch meet the 1 ms deadline, including any interference from prewarming and the swap? Second, did that tick have exactly one latch occurrence? An on-time duplicate fails the second question; one late latch can satisfy the count but fail the first. The hypothesis aims for both, so neither should be inferred from the other.
What if prewarming itself takes substantial time?

Then moving work before cutover has not necessarily removed its effect on the control path. The hypothesis needs prewarming to coexist with the ongoing 1-ms ticks without disrupting their deadlines or latches. It also needs the candidate code and state to remain suitable for selection at the eventual boundary. The statement supplies neither an execution-time bound nor a method for maintaining candidate-state coherence, so those remain matters to establish.
Does this hypothesis also establish safe state-schema migration and reset recovery?

No. Prewarming candidate state does not by itself validate a state-schema migration, and ordering cutover after a latch acknowledgment does not by itself ensure recovery of a compatible firmware-state pair after a reset. The candidate still needs to be a compatible pair before selection, and reset recovery needs its own recoverable pair-selection rule. This hypothesis concerns the timing and once-per-tick latch behavior of cutover.
What is the most careful one-sentence statement of the hypothesis?

‘We hypothesize that prewarming the candidate code and state, prioritizing the latch interrupt over cutover, and switching firmware-state pairs only after acknowledgment of the relevant latch will allow each 1-ms tick to latch exactly once while meeting its deadline.’ The acknowledgment’s meaning, the tick boundary, and the timing and latch outcomes still need to be established.

I want to replay the SwapStress-10k report workloads with candidate code and state prewarmed and cutover gated on acknowledgment. Across 10,000 swaps, we'll measure physical actuator latch intervals and deadline misses. How should I describe this activity?

Describe it as a replay and measurement activity, not as a result: replay the workloads represented in the SwapStress-10k report using prewarming and acknowledgment-gated cutover, and measure physical latch intervals and deadline misses across 10,000 swaps. Those measurements address whether the proposed cutover ordering delivers timely physical latching. No latch interval or missed-deadline count has been observed in this activity yet.
Why use the report workloads rather than just describe this as another set of swaps?

‘Replay the SwapStress-10k report workloads’ identifies the workload basis for the activity. It distinguishes the conditions being replayed from the cutover behavior being examined: candidate prewarming and acknowledgment-gated switching. It does not mean the replay will reproduce identical timing observations. The new measurements concern physical latch intervals and deadline misses during its own 10,000 swaps.
Does the count of 10,000 refer to latch events or swaps?

Swaps. The activity measures physical latch intervals and deadline misses *across 10,000 swaps*; it does not state a total count of ticks or physical latch events. Keep the number attached to swaps when describing the run.
What does prewarming contribute to this replay?

It is one of the proposed cutover conditions being exercised: candidate code and state are prepared ahead of selection so the boundary need not take on all of that preparation work. The replay can then measure what happens at physical latching under that arrangement. Prewarming is not itself a measured result, and the activity does not specify a particular method or duration for it.
And what exactly makes the cutover ‘acknowledgment-gated’?

The swap is conditional on acknowledgment of the latch obligation relevant to the boundary. The intent is not to change the selected firmware-state pair while that obligation remains unresolved. For the replay to be interpretable, the acknowledgment must be associated with the relevant tick and must mean what the cutover rule assumes it means. The activity names the gating condition but does not prescribe an acknowledgment implementation.
Should the latch interrupt still have priority over cutover during the replay?

That is part of the cutover hypothesis the replay is meant to evaluate: prewarming, latch-interrupt priority over cutover, and swapping after acknowledgment are the proposed ordering. The activity specifically calls out prewarming and acknowledgment-gated cutover. When describing the run, keep clear which proposed conditions are actually exercised rather than treating a measured latch interval as proof of an unstated priority configuration.
What is a ‘physical latch interval’ here?

It is an interval measured with respect to physical actuator latch events, rather than the issuance of command IDs or the timing of firmware dispatch alone. To interpret the resulting measurements, define which latch events bound an interval and relate those events to the affected ticks and swaps. The activity does not supply an instrumentation method or observed interval values, so neither should be assumed.
If consecutive physical latch events are 1 ms apart, would that show each tick latched once?

Not by itself. An interval between two observed events says how far apart they were; it does not automatically establish which ticks they belong to or rule out an additional latch event elsewhere. Likewise, if an expected latch never occurs, there may be no event at that point from which to form the intended interval. Relating the physical events to ticks is necessary before using the interval measurements to assess once-per-1-ms-tick behavior.
Are deadline misses the same measurement as physical latch intervals?

No. A physical latch interval concerns spacing between latch events. A deadline miss concerns whether a tick’s required action occurred by its 1 ms deadline. An interval can help reveal irregular timing, but determining a miss requires the appropriate tick boundary and deadline association. Record and interpret the two quantities separately rather than deriving every deadline outcome solely from spacing.
Where in the replay should the measurements be associated with each swap?

Keep enough ordering to identify the latch behavior at the cutover boundary and on the immediately following tick, as well as the relevant deadline outcomes. The 10,000 swaps are the units across which the activity measures behavior, so a physical latch observation needs a defensible relationship to its swap and tick. The activity does not specify a particular trace format.
Could a swap be requested but held back while waiting for acknowledgment?

Acknowledgment-gated cutover means a requested switch cannot be treated as completed before its gating condition is satisfied. In counting 10,000 swaps, distinguish actual cutovers from requests that are still waiting. A wait may also matter to the timing observations, but the activity does not say that any wait has occurred or provide its duration.
Would a late acknowledgment necessarily count as a deadline miss?

That depends on which tick the acknowledgment covers and what event marks completion of its required latch. The measurement should determine deadline misses from the relevant tick and physical latch timing, not from the mere fact that a cutover waits. Gating may prevent a premature swap, but waiting does not retroactively make a late latch timely.
If the physical latch intervals look regular, can we conclude there were no deadline misses?

Not without relating the latch events to the deadlines of their assigned ticks. Regular spacing and timely placement are different questions: a sequence of evenly spaced events could still be offset relative to when the ticks require them. That is why the activity calls for measuring both physical latch intervals and deadline misses.
What if the replay shows no deadline misses but there are two latches for one tick?

Then meeting the deadlines would not settle the once-per-tick question. Two physical latches assigned to one tick would conflict with the proposed ‘each 1-ms tick latches once’ behavior even if both occurred before a deadline. The physical-event record needs enough tick association to distinguish one timely latch from an extra latch; a deadline-miss count alone cannot do that. This is a possible interpretation to prepare for, not an observed outcome.
Do the report’s actuator sequence traces replace the physical latch measurements?

No. The report workloads supply the basis for the replay, but the specified measurements in this activity are physical latch intervals and deadline misses. A command sequence trace records events at its own observation point; it should not be substituted for physical latch timing without an established correspondence. The replay is intended to observe the physical latch path directly enough to assess those quantities.
Does this activity include state-migration rejection or reset recovery testing?

Not as stated. It replays the SwapStress-10k report workloads with prewarming and acknowledgment-gated cutover, measuring physical latch intervals and deadline misses across 10,000 swaps. It does not specify an incompatible migration, atomic rejection check, update-time reset, or recovery-pair check. Its scope is the cutover’s physical latch timing and deadline behavior.
How should I write the run instruction without suggesting the measurements have already passed?

‘Replay the SwapStress-10k report workloads with candidate code and state prewarmed and cutover gated on acknowledgment. Across 10,000 completed swaps, measure physical actuator latch intervals and deadline misses, retaining their association with the relevant ticks and swap boundaries.’ That states the activity and what to observe without asserting any result.
Revised SwapStress-10k measured a 0.94-ms maximum latch interval, zero missed deadlines, and 10,000 consecutive acknowledged actuator commands. How should I report those results?

Report the three observations separately: ‘Revised SwapStress-10k measured a maximum physical latch interval of 0.94 ms, recorded zero missed deadlines, and recorded 10,000 consecutive acknowledged actuator commands.’ That preserves what was measured without treating latch spacing, deadline compliance, and command acknowledgment as interchangeable.
Is 0.94 ms the time taken by the firmware-state-pair swap?

No. It is the maximum *latch interval* measured in the revised run. The result does not give a maximum swap duration or dispatch latency. Keep the event being timed in the description so that 0.94 ms is not attributed to a different part of cutover.
How does that maximum compare with the 1 ms control period?

The measured maximum latch interval is 0.06 ms below 1 ms. That comparison describes the observed spacing of physical latch events. The separately reported zero missed deadlines is the observation about deadlines; a maximum interval alone would not necessarily show where each latch fell relative to its tick’s deadline.
Does ‘zero missed deadlines’ mean there were no timing problems anywhere in the controller?

It means no deadline misses were recorded in this revised SwapStress-10k measurement. It does not characterize every timing event elsewhere in the controller or guarantee the same outcome in every future run. State it with the run’s scope rather than as an unrestricted property of the system.
What does ‘10,000 consecutive acknowledged actuator commands’ add beyond the latch-interval measurement?

It describes command progression and acknowledgment, while the latch-interval measurement describes physical timing between latch events. The result reports a consecutive run of 10,000 acknowledged actuator commands. It does not say that the number 10,000 is the count of measured latch intervals, nor should acknowledgment be silently substituted for a physical latch observation.
Does ‘consecutive’ establish that no command sequence position was missing within those 10,000?

It describes the acknowledged actuator commands as consecutive, so there is no reported gap in that acknowledged progression. The wording does not, on its own, define how commands are assigned to individual ticks or establish that every possible actuator effect was observed. Keep the conclusion attached to the acknowledged sequence.
Can I infer that each 1-ms tick latched exactly once?

That is the intended cutover behavior, but these figures should be reported at the level they state. The 0.94-ms maximum describes latch intervals; zero missed deadlines describes the recorded deadline outcomes; and 10,000 consecutive acknowledged commands describes the acknowledged progression. To make an exactly-once-per-tick statement from them, the observations must establish which physical latch belongs to each tick and exclude an additional latch for that same tick. Do not replace that association with the command count alone.
Is it reasonable to present the measurements together when discussing acknowledgment-gated cutover?

Yes. They provide complementary observations from Revised SwapStress-10k: physical latch spacing, deadline outcomes, and acknowledged command progression. Presenting them together makes the cutover behavior easier to assess, provided the report still distinguishes what each quantity measures and does not claim an unreported cause or broader guarantee.
Does the result tell us whether candidate code and state were prewarmed in the replay?

The replay activity used prewarming and acknowledgment-gated cutover. The result reports measurements from that revised run; it does not separately quantify how much time prewarming saved or isolate the contribution of either condition. You can identify the run conditions without assigning a measured benefit to one of them.
Should I say the 10,000 acknowledged commands correspond one-to-one with the 10,000 swaps?

No. The result specifies 10,000 consecutive acknowledged actuator commands, while the replay activity covers 10,000 swaps. Equal counts do not establish that each swap corresponds to exactly one acknowledged command. Those are different counted events, and the report should keep them separate.
What if I describe 0.94 ms as a worst-case guarantee?

That would overstate it. ‘Maximum measured latch interval’ or ‘maximum observed latch interval in Revised SwapStress-10k’ is accurate. The result does not establish a guaranteed bound for every future update or every operating condition.
Can these measurements settle state-schema compatibility and update-time reset recovery?

No. They report latch timing, deadline misses, and acknowledged actuator commands in the revised run. They do not report an incompatible state-migration check or the firmware-state pair recovered after an update-time reset. Those requirements cannot be inferred from these cutover measurements.
Give me a concise finding that does not blur the three observations.
In Revised SwapStress-10k, the maximum measured physical latch interval was 0.94 ms, there were zero recorded deadline misses, and 10,000 actuator commands were acknowledged consecutively.

For state-schema changes and reset recovery, I propose validating shadow migrations before atomically committing a versioned firmware-state pair. After a reset, the controller would boot the last committed compatible pair. How should I spell out that proposal?

Make the firmware-state pair the unit of validation, commitment, and recovery. Prepare migrated state separately as a shadow candidate, validate that the candidate firmware can use it, and do not commit the candidate if that validation fails. If validation succeeds, atomically commit the versioned firmware and its compatible state as one pair. After any update-time reset, select the last committed compatible pair for boot.

‘Atomically’ is important at the commitment boundary: recovery must not see candidate firmware with a different pair’s state, or candidate state with different firmware. This describes the proposed behavior; it does not yet establish that a particular storage or boot mechanism implements it.
What does ‘shadow migration’ add? Why not migrate the active state in place?

A shadow migration lets the candidate state be prepared and examined without partially replacing the state used by the active firmware. If the migration proves incompatible, the proposed rejection is straightforward: do not commit the candidate pair, and leave the active pair intact. An in-place transformation would make that atomic-rejection obligation harder to express because validation could encounter a partly transformed active state.

‘Shadow’ does not by itself guarantee that the migrated state stays coherent while control continues. The state being committed still has to correspond to a coherent point at which the new pair can take responsibility.
When you say ‘validate,’ is successful decoding enough?

No. The validation needed here is compatibility between the candidate firmware and the shadow-migrated state, not merely readability of the representation. The pair must be suitable for execution together after commitment and, if necessary, after reset. The proposal does not specify particular schemas or acceptance rules, so it cannot declare a migration compatible merely because a decoder accepts its fields.
What is the version for if the pair has already been validated?

Versioning identifies which firmware and state belong to the same committed pair. It gives the commitment and recovery rules an unambiguous object to select. A matching version label is not, on its own, proof of compatibility: validation must establish that before commitment. Conversely, recovery should not combine individually available components just because each has some recognizable version information.
Do firmware and migrated state have to become committed in exactly the same physical write?

The proposal requires an atomic *observable commitment of the pair*, not necessarily a single physical write. The key question is what boot and control can select if execution or power is interrupted at any point. Before the commitment is complete, an incomplete candidate must not be selectable as the new committed pair. Once it is complete, recovery must be able to identify firmware and compatible state together.

How to obtain that property depends on the storage and reset behavior. No particular write sequence is specified by this proposal.
Suppose validation fails after most of the candidate state has been prepared. What is the atomic rejection?

The candidate firmware-state pair is not committed or selected for control. Partially prepared shadow data remains outside the selected pair; it cannot change the active state merely because preparation progressed far. That is the atomicity required of rejection: incompatibility does not produce a partly migrated, partly active controller.

The proposal does not require treating shadow preparation itself as an all-or-nothing operation. It requires that a failed candidate cannot have a partial effect on which firmware-state pair is active or recoverable as committed.
What if the active state changes between shadow validation and the proposed commit?

Validation of a shadow state at one moment is not sufficient if the state selected at commitment no longer represents the required control state. The proposal needs the candidate state that is ultimately committed to be coherent and compatible at that boundary. That may require checking the final candidate against the relevant state at commitment, or otherwise establishing that intervening changes are accounted for.

The node does not choose a mechanism for maintaining that coherence. The essential constraint is that ‘validated’ applies to the state actually paired with the committed firmware, not only to an earlier shadow snapshot.
If the new pair is committed, can the controller just boot whichever state happens to be available after a reset?

No. Recovery is explicitly pair-based: boot the last committed *compatible firmware-state pair*. Availability of firmware and availability of state as separate items do not authorize mixing them. A reset during the update must not turn a partial candidate into the selected pair or attach a state to firmware for which compatibility has not been established.
Can you walk through resets before and after the atomic commitment, without assuming any particular storage technology?

Before a candidate pair has been atomically committed, a reset must leave recovery able to boot the last committed compatible pair. If the candidate has been committed as a complete, compatible pair, recovery can select that committed pair. For a reset during the commitment process, recovery needs a clear answer to whether the new pair was committed; it must not assemble a half-committed combination.

The precise point at which the answer changes is an implementation matter. What matters to the proposal is that every possible update-time reset has a compatible committed pair to boot and an unambiguous way to identify it.
Does ‘last committed compatible pair’ mean we can promote an unvalidated pair and check it during boot?

No. The proposed order is validate the shadow migration *before* committing the versioned pair. Boot-time selection of the last committed compatible pair relies on commitment meaning that the pair was already established as compatible. A candidate awaiting validation, or one that failed validation, must not be treated as a committed pair merely because its files or state are present.
What happens if the reset occurs while validation is still running?

Validation in progress does not constitute commitment. Recovery should boot the last committed compatible pair rather than the unfinished candidate. The proposal leaves open how incomplete shadow work is identified or handled afterward; it does not need that work to be bootable in order to satisfy the recovery rule.
Is an atomic commit enough if the code and state are stored together but boot selection can see an incomplete update?

No. Atomicity has to cover the selection that matters to recovery. If boot can mistake an incomplete pair for the last committed one, storing its components near each other does not achieve the proposed behavior. The firmware, its state, and the fact of their commitment must be interpreted together so that a reset at any point produces a compatible selection.

This is a statement of the required observable guarantee, not a prescription for how to encode it.
How do I distinguish the pair's version from the firmware's internal state-schema version?

For this proposal, ‘versioned firmware-state pair’ means recovery can identify the committed association between the firmware and the state validated for it. A schema may have its own version information, but a schema label alone would not say which complete pair was atomically committed. No particular number of version fields or encoding is specified; the design must simply avoid selecting incompatible components independently.
Should the old pair be erased as soon as the shadow migration validates?

Validation alone is not the atomic commitment of the new pair. The recovery rule requires the last committed compatible pair to remain bootable through an update-time reset, including a reset before the new commitment is complete. Any treatment of the earlier committed pair must preserve that rule. This proposal does not prescribe when storage can be reclaimed.
What if the candidate is compatible in memory but not fully recoverable after reset?

Then it does not yet meet the proposed conditions for atomic commitment as a recoverable pair. Compatibility during execution and availability for boot after an update-time reset are both relevant. The new firmware and its corresponding state must be ready to be selected together after reset before the commitment can safely make them the last committed compatible pair.
Does this proposal guarantee that every control tick still meets its 1 ms deadline during validation and commit?

Not by itself. Shadow validation and atomic commitment address migration rejection and firmware-state pairing. Their work must still coexist with uninterrupted 1 ms control deadlines and actuator consistency. Calling migration ‘shadow’ or commitment ‘atomic’ does not establish that either operation has no timing interference with control.
And does booting a compatible pair mean actuator commands continued without interruption during the reset?

No. Booting the last committed compatible pair is the specified recovery behavior after a reset. It does not assert that control ran during the reset or that actuator-command timing across the reset remained uninterrupted. The uninterrupted-update deadline and command requirements and the after-reset compatibility requirement should be evaluated according to their respective conditions.
What is the shortest useful statement of the proposal and its two failure cases?

Validate a shadow migration for the candidate firmware, then atomically commit the compatible, versioned firmware-state pair. If validation fails, reject the candidate without partially changing the active pair. If an update-time reset occurs at any point, boot the last committed compatible pair, never an incomplete or mismatched combination. The specific validation, commitment, and boot-selection mechanisms remain to be defined.
I want to test shadow-migration rejection, inject resets at dual-slot commit boundaries, and then verify compatible recovery and gap-free 1-ms actuator ticks. How should I structure that plan?

Keep the three checks distinct but connected. First, present an incompatible shadow migration and check that rejection leaves the selected firmware-state pair unchanged, with no partial promotion. Second, inject resets at the dual-slot commit boundaries and check which complete firmware-state pair recovery selects. Third, examine actuator ticks during uninterrupted portions of the update and after recovery for the applicable 1 ms timing and no-gap behavior.

For every reset case, the required recovery result is a compatible firmware-state pair. ‘Gap-free 1-ms actuator ticks’ must be scoped carefully: a reset interrupts execution, so the plan should not assume that control ticks continue through the reset itself.
What should the shadow-migration rejection test actually establish?

It should establish that an incompatible shadow migration cannot become a partly selected pair. If validation rejects the candidate, the active firmware and its state should remain the pair responsible for control, and the candidate state should not be treated as committed or available for recovery as a compatible pair.

The test also needs to observe the uninterrupted control path while rejection happens: rejecting a migration must not create a late 1 ms tick or a missing actuator command. The plan does not specify a particular incompatible schema, so the test case must have a defined reason it is incompatible without assuming any specific fields here.
Would it be enough to check that the migration function returns an error?

No. An error return says what the migration reported; atomic rejection concerns what the controller actually selected and what remained recoverable. Check that the candidate was not partially committed, that the active firmware-state pair remained coherent, and that control continued under a compatible pair. Otherwise, an error could coexist with a partial state change.
What is meant by a ‘dual-slot commit boundary’ in this test plan?

It is a point in the transition where the dual-slot arrangement may change which complete firmware-state pair is treated as committed. The reset injections should probe the boundaries where interruption could affect that determination. The exact storage operations and the number of distinct boundaries are not specified, so the plan should identify them from the implementation rather than assume a particular write sequence.

At each chosen boundary, the recovery check asks the same question: did boot select a complete, compatible pair rather than mixing firmware from one slot with state from the other?
If a reset lands before the new pair is committed, what result should I expect?

Recovery should select the last committed compatible firmware-state pair. A candidate that is still being prepared or validated must not become bootable merely because some of its contents are present. Which slot supplies the last committed pair depends on the state of the proposed implementation at that injection point; compatibility and completed commitment are what matter.
And if the reset occurs right at the commit boundary?

That is the critical ambiguity to test. Recovery must resolve the interrupted operation to a committed compatible pair. It can select a complete earlier committed pair if the new commitment did not take effect, or a complete new pair if it did. It must not select a combination whose firmware and state were not committed together.

The test should not infer the expected side of the boundary from elapsed time alone. It should use the implementation’s defined commitment rule to judge whether the recovered pair is valid.
Does injecting one reset at each boundary prove recovery after any update-time reset?

It is a useful test, but the phrase ‘after any update-time reset’ is broader than a small collection of injections. The plan should identify the update-time states and commit boundaries that can be interrupted, then assess whether the recovery rule covers them. A finite set of successful reset tests supplies observations; the argument for *any* update-time reset also depends on the completeness of the boundary model and the guarantees of the commit mechanism.
Should I check the firmware version after reboot, or the state version?

Check the recovered firmware-state *pair* and its compatibility. A firmware version alone would not establish that the state booted with it is the one validated and committed for that firmware. A state version alone would have the corresponding problem. The dual-slot recovery check is about selecting a complete compatible pair, not merely finding recognizable versions in storage.
Where do gap-free actuator ticks fit relative to the reset injections?

There are two observations to keep separate. During uninterrupted update execution—including a failed shadow migration or an attempted cutover—the 1 ms control deadlines and required actuator commands must continue without gaps. In reset-injection cases, execution is interrupted; after recovery, check that the recovered compatible pair resumes its applicable tick and actuator obligations without an avoidable replay or gap in the observed running sequence.

Do not report a continuous stream of on-time ticks *through* a reset unless that stronger behavior is explicitly required and measured. This plan states compatible recovery after reset, not uninterrupted execution during one.
Would contiguous command IDs be enough to call the actuator ticks gap-free?

Not by themselves. The intended check concerns actuator ticks and commands, not just the numbering of issued IDs. For each applicable 1 ms tick, establish whether its required actuator action occurred, whether it met the deadline, and whether an output was repeated or a command was skipped. A contiguous ID trace can help locate sequence positions, but it cannot substitute for observing the relevant actuator behavior.
Does ‘gap-free’ also rule out duplicated commands?

The overall control requirement rules out both skipped and duplicated actuator commands. ‘Gap-free’ highlights the no-skipped side, but the tick check should not declare success if a tick has an extra effective command or a repeated output. Examine the two properties separately: no required tick lacks its command, and no tick produces an unauthorized additional one, while uninterrupted ticks meet their 1 ms deadlines.
Can the reset cases be combined with the incompatible-migration case?

They can be considered together where the implementation permits it, but keep the expected observations explicit.
