If the reset interrupts the operation that establishes that boundary, boot still needs an unambiguous way to select one complete committed pair—not a partially combined one.

The precise point where the new commitment takes effect has to be defined by the eventual persistence mechanism; elapsed time near the reset is not enough to define it.
Is it acceptable if boot sometimes chooses the previous pair and sometimes the candidate after resets at what looks like the same instant?

The externally described instant may not reveal whether commitment took effect. Either outcome can be consistent with the proposal if, in each case, boot selects a complete pair that was validly committed under a defined rule. What would not be acceptable is an outcome with no established commitment, an incompatible firmware-state combination, or an ambiguous rule that cannot explain which pair was selected.
Does an interrupted versioned record necessarily mean the candidate state itself is corrupt?

No. The question concerns boot's ability to establish that a compatible pair was committed. Candidate state might be readable without its commitment being complete, or the record might be incomplete without telling us anything conclusive about every candidate component. Boot should not infer a completed pair merely from the apparent condition of one component. The selection rule needs evidence about the pair and its commitment.
What must the previous committed pair retain during this process?

It must remain recoverable for a reset that occurs before the candidate becomes recoverably committed. Otherwise boot could face an incomplete new record with no compatible committed pair to select. The proposal's after-reset requirement depends on there being a complete compatible fallback until the new pair can take its place under the commit rule. That states an obligation, not a particular storage layout.
Could boot perform the unfinished state migration itself and then select the candidate?

That would be a different recovery behavior from simply identifying and booting the last committed compatible pair. Presence of an unfinished migration is not evidence that it would complete or validate successfully after reset. Under the stated proposal, boot must not treat an uncommitted candidate as committed by finishing or assuming the missing step. Any additional boot-time migration scheme would require its own explicit compatibility and recovery guarantees.
Where does compatibility enter if boot already has a valid commit record?

The commitment is supposed to refer to a firmware-state pair whose shadow migration was validated before commit. Boot must use the record to select *that* associated pair, rather than independently choosing a firmware item and a state item that merely happen to exist. Validating a commit record answers whether commitment completed; selecting the correctly associated firmware and state answers which pair it committed. Both are needed to support compatible recovery.
Does boot need to repeat the entire schema validation on every reset?

The question does not require a particular boot-time validation procedure. The proposed order places shadow-migration validation before commitment, so boot needs a trustworthy way to recognize and select the pair that was validly committed on that basis. Repeating validation might be part of a particular design, but it cannot substitute for establishing whether the interrupted commit actually took effect.
Would two separate records, one naming firmware and one naming state, meet the requirement?

Not simply because both records are individually readable. Boot would need an unambiguous rule establishing that the two records belong to the same committed compatible pair, even if a reset occurred between changes to them. If it could observe a new firmware selection alongside an old state selection, the proposed pair-level atomicity would be lost. The number of records is an implementation choice; their observable pairing is the requirement.
What if boot finds two records that each appear complete?

It must apply a defined selection rule that identifies the last committed compatible pair. Each apparent record needs to be assessed as a complete commitment of an associated firmware-state pair; then boot can determine which valid commitment governs. The rule cannot choose components independently or assume that the record encountered first, or one with a larger version label, is necessarily the last valid commitment.
Can you give me a simple way to describe the ambiguous case?

Suppose a reset occurs while the candidate pair's versioned commitment is being recorded. On restart, some information about that candidate may be visible. The ambiguity is whether the record became a complete commitment before interruption. Boot must resolve that question according to a defined persistence rule: if the candidate was not committed, select the retained last committed compatible pair; if it was, select the complete candidate pair. It must never treat partial visibility as permission to mix the two.
Would a checksum alone resolve that ambiguity?

Not necessarily. An integrity check might help detect incomplete or altered information, but it does not by itself define when a pair becomes committed, which firmware and state the commitment covers, or which of two valid committed pairs is last. Those meanings and the storage behavior on interrupted writes would need to be specified. No particular checksum or commit-record mechanism is selected by this question.
How would we assess whether a proposed boot-selection rule really covers any update-time reset?

Consider every point at which reset can interrupt preparation, validation, recording, and selection. For each resulting persistent state, ask whether boot can identify a complete last committed compatible pair without relying on an unfinished record. Pay particular attention to interruption while the versioned commit record changes: that is where apparent candidate information could be mistaken for a completed commitment.

A finite set of reset tests can supply observations, but the ‘any update-time reset’ claim also needs an argument grounded in what the storage and commit operations actually guarantee.
Does successfully booting compatible firmware and state also prove the 1-ms actuator sequence remained uninterrupted through the reset?

No. Boot selection answers which compatible firmware-state pair runs after recovery. A reset interrupts execution, so it is not evidence that 1-ms control ticks or actuator commands continued while the controller was reset. The recovery rule should not be used to claim an uninterrupted actuator sequence through that interval.
What's the shortest answer to the original boot question?

Boot must accept only a complete, valid commitment that identifies firmware and compatible state as one versioned pair. If reset interrupts the new commit record before that commitment takes effect, boot selects the retained last committed compatible pair; if the new commitment took effect, it selects the complete new pair. The persistence rule must make that distinction unambiguous without relying on partly written fields.

My hypothesis is that dual CRC-protected records and immutable A/B manifests let boot select the newest fully committed, schema-compatible firmware-state pair after a reset. Does that address an interrupted versioned commit record?

It is a concrete hypothesis for resolving that ambiguity. The immutable A/B manifests would identify candidate firmware-state pairs and their schema associations, while the two CRC-protected records would provide information for boot to assess commitment. Boot would select the newest pair only among those it can establish are fully committed and schema-compatible.

The key point remains to be demonstrated: a reset at any point in the update must not make a partial record look like authority to select an incomplete or incompatible pair. Having two records and CRC protection is not, by itself, proof of that property.
What role do the A/B manifests play if the commit records already name a version?

The manifests are intended to give a stable description of what each A/B firmware-state pair contains and how its firmware and state relate. A version in a commit record can identify a selection, but boot still needs to know which complete pair that selection refers to and whether its schema is compatible. The hypothesis relies on immutable manifests so an interrupted commitment cannot change the meaning of a pair's description partway through recovery.

It does not specify the manifest fields or the method of establishing compatibility; those would need to be defined in a concrete design.
Does ‘immutable’ mean the manifests can never be updated?

Here it means that, while a particular A or B manifest is being used to identify a candidate or committed pair, boot must be able to treat that manifest as stable. It should not read a partly changed description and mistake it for the manifest of a complete pair. The hypothesis does not state a lifetime policy for the slots or prescribe how a later update would prepare a new manifest.
Why are there two CRC-protected records rather than one?

The proposed dual records are intended to leave boot a way to distinguish a complete commitment from an interrupted change and still identify a committed pair. If one record is incomplete after a reset, another valid record could retain the information needed for selection. But whether that works depends on the update rule: both records must not become unusable at once, and boot must be able to interpret their ordering and validity without guessing.

The hypothesis names the two records; it does not yet specify how they are written or establish that their failure behavior provides the intended fallback.
Would a valid CRC mean a record is definitely fully committed?

No. A CRC is an integrity check on recorded data under whatever format the design defines. Passing that check alone does not establish that the record represents a completed commitment, that the referenced A/B manifest is complete, or that its firmware and state are schema-compatible. The boot rule needs an explicit meaning of ‘fully committed’ in addition to CRC validity.
If both records pass their CRC checks, can boot just choose the one with the higher version number?

Only if the defined ordering shows that its referenced pair was fully committed and schema-compatible. A CRC-valid record could still be irrelevant to a completed commitment under the proposed rules. ‘Newest’ is a selection criterion *among qualifying pairs*, not a license to select whichever readable record has the largest version label. Boot must also associate the selected record with its complete immutable manifest and the matching firmware and state.
What would make the firmware and state ‘schema-compatible’ for that selection?

The selected firmware must be able to use the state identified with it under the applicable schema rules. The hypothesis proposes using the A/B manifests as stable pair descriptions, but a matching label alone cannot establish that a migration actually produced valid state. Compatibility must have been established for the pair that became committed, and boot's selection must preserve that association.

No particular schema fields or validation algorithm are specified here, so the hypothesis cannot declare compatibility from a version number or a CRC alone.
Suppose reset interrupts the new record and only part of it is readable. What should boot do?

Boot must not treat the readable part as a completed commitment. It should assess the records and manifests according to a rule that admits only fully committed, schema-compatible pairs, then select the newest qualifying pair. If the interrupted candidate does not qualify, it must not be selected merely because some candidate fields survived.

The hypothesis requires that a qualifying pair remain identifiable in that situation; the precise way the two records provide it is still to be specified and tested.
And if a reset occurs after the new record becomes fully committed?

Then, assuming the referenced immutable manifest and its firmware-state pair meet the compatibility conditions, the new pair can qualify as the newest fully committed, schema-compatible pair. The challenge is defining a recoverable boundary that separates this case from a merely partial record. A reset near that boundary cannot justify mixing the previous pair's state with the new pair's firmware.
Could the two CRC-protected records disagree after an interrupted update?

That is a case the boot rule must handle rather than assume away. If the records point to different A/B pairs, boot needs to determine which complete commitments each represents and select the newest qualifying pair. If a record is incomplete or cannot be trusted under the defined rule, it must not make its pair eligible merely by disagreeing with the other record. The hypothesis does not state what any particular reset will leave in either record.
Do immutable manifests by themselves tell boot which of A and B is newest?

No. A manifest describes an A/B pair; immutability prevents its meaning from changing during selection. Determining which pair was most recently *fully committed* is a separate question for the commitment information and its ordering rule. Boot needs both: a reliable pair description and a reliable selection among completed commitments.
Is a fully committed pair necessarily the same as an active pair before the reset?

Those concepts should not be conflated. ‘Active’ describes what was selected for running control at an observation point; ‘fully committed’ describes what recovery can establish as a completed, compatible pair after a reset. The hypothesis says boot chooses the newest fully committed schema-compatible pair. It does not say that a transient observation of activity, by itself, establishes a recoverable commitment.
Could boot combine firmware from A with state from B if their schema versions match?

Not under this pair-selection hypothesis. Boot selects a *firmware-state pair* identified by a qualifying A/B manifest and commitment, rather than independently choosing components with apparently matching schema versions. Schema compatibility is necessary, but the components also have to be the ones belonging to the selected fully committed pair.
What if neither CRC-protected record appears to identify a fully committed compatible pair?

That would expose a gap in the proposed recovery mechanism: the hypothesis aims to let boot identify such a pair after an update-time reset. Boot must not invent one by accepting a partial record or combining mismatched components. To establish the hypothesis, the update and persistence rules need to show that every reachable reset state leaves at least one qualifying pair identifiable. The node does not specify another fallback for a state in which none qualifies.
Does this hypothesis say boot should finish a partially written commit during startup?

No. It proposes selecting the newest *fully committed* compatible pair. A partially written record is not automatically eligible, and finishing an interrupted candidate would be a separate behavior needing its own defined safety conditions. The selection rule can use the last qualifying pair without promoting a candidate whose commitment was interrupted.
How would you evaluate this hypothesis without assuming a particular storage technology?

Define the validity and ordering rules for the two CRC-protected records and the completeness and compatibility conditions for each immutable A/B manifest. Then consider reset after every point where the records or candidate pair can change. For each resulting readable state, determine whether boot can identify at least one fully committed schema-compatible pair and select the newest such pair without mixing components.

That describes the reasoning to perform, not a completed reset test. Its conclusion would also depend on the real storage guarantees for interrupted writes; CRC protection and two records cannot supply guarantees that the underlying medium does not provide.
Would verifying the CRCs and the manifest settle the 1-ms actuator deadlines after reboot?

No. Those checks address pair selection after reset. They do not measure latch timing or show that control met a 1-ms deadline, and a reset itself interrupts execution. Keep the compatible-recovery claim separate from deadline and actuator-sequence observations during uninterrupted updates.
Can you phrase the hypothesis succinctly while preserving that uncertainty?

‘We hypothesize that dual CRC-protected commit records, together with immutable A/B manifests identifying compatible firmware-state pairs, allow boot after an update-time reset to select the newest fully committed, schema-compatible pair. The record-validity, commitment, and ordering rules must still be shown to work when reset interrupts a record.’

Let's run BootCut-512 with byte-boundary resets across both commit records. After each reset, check whether boot selects the newest CRC-valid, schema-compatible firmware-state pair. How should I state the activity?

State it as a reset-injection test: ‘Run BootCut-512, injecting resets at byte boundaries across both commit records. After each reset, check that boot selects the newest CRC-valid, schema-compatible firmware-state pair.’ This identifies the interruption points and the boot-selection check without claiming that any reset has been injected or that recovery has passed.
What does ‘across both commit records’ require us to cover?

The reset points must cover byte boundaries in each of the two records, not only one of them. For every tested interruption, examine the record state available on reboot and the pair boot actually selects. The activity does not specify the records’ sizes, layout, or write order, so those details should be taken from the implementation rather than assumed here.
Why use byte-boundary resets instead of resetting only before and after a record is written?

A reset at a byte boundary probes an intermediate record state that a before-or-after check might miss. Those intermediate states are relevant to whether boot mistakes an interrupted record for a usable one. The test still has to use the actual record-validity rules: the fact that a reset was placed at a byte boundary does not, by itself, say what data survived or which pair is eligible.
Does the name BootCut-512 mean we should report exactly 512 successful recoveries?

No outcome follows from the test’s name. The stated activity is BootCut-512 with byte-boundary resets across both commit records. It does not report a count of successful recoveries, or even a result for any injection. Report the number of resets actually exercised and their outcomes only when those observations are available.
What should the check do if one commit record passes its CRC and the other does not?

It should evaluate whether the CRC-valid record identifies a schema-compatible firmware-state pair and whether that pair is the newest eligible one under the defined selection rule. The record that fails its CRC should not be treated as a valid basis for selecting a pair merely because some of its fields remain readable. The expected boot choice cannot be named in advance without knowing the records’ contents and ordering at that reset point.
And if both records pass their CRC checks?

Check the pairs each record identifies, establish schema compatibility for each, and determine which qualifying pair is newest. Boot should select that pair as a unit. Two passing CRCs alone do not tell you which pair is newer, nor do they authorize choosing firmware from one record and state from the other.
Could a CRC-valid record still be inappropriate for boot?

Yes. CRC validity addresses the record’s integrity under the chosen CRC check; the referenced firmware-state pair also has to be schema-compatible. In addition, if ‘fully committed’ is part of the intended recovery rule, the implementation must establish how record validity relates to completed commitment. The BootCut-512 check is stated as selection of the newest CRC-valid, schema-compatible pair; it should not silently treat a passing CRC as proof of any additional, undefined commitment condition.
How do we check schema compatibility without relying only on a version number?

Use the implementation’s defined compatibility rule for the firmware and state identified together by the record and its pair description. A version number may help identify what is being checked, but its magnitude alone does not establish that the firmware can use that state. The activity does not specify a schema or validation algorithm, so the test description should name the compatibility check without inventing its internals.
When you say ‘newest,’ newest among which records?

Among the candidate firmware-state pairs that qualify under the test’s stated criteria: their commit records are CRC-valid and the pairs they identify are schema-compatible. A more recent-looking but CRC-invalid record should not win, and a CRC-valid record pointing to an incompatible pair should not win. How the records establish relative recency must be defined by the implementation; it cannot be inferred from which record boot reads first.
Is the expected selection necessarily the pair that was running immediately before the reset?

Not necessarily. The test’s expected selection is the newest qualifying pair established from the persistent records and their associated firmware and state. Which pair was running before the reset is a different observation; it does not by itself establish what was recoverably recorded when the reset occurred.
What should we capture for each byte-boundary reset so the outcome can be interpreted?

Identify the record and byte boundary at which reset was injected; establish what boot could read from both records after reset; apply the CRC and schema-compatibility checks; determine the newest qualifying firmware-state pair; and compare that expected pair with the pair boot selected. Those are the observations needed to explain a selection. This does not prescribe a particular record format or logging mechanism.
Would it suffice to check that boot starts successfully?

No. Booting something does not establish that it selected the *newest CRC-valid, schema-compatible firmware-state pair*. The check needs the identities of firmware and state selected together, plus the eligibility and ordering of the available pair records. A successful start with an older qualifying pair, or with mismatched components, would not satisfy the selection criterion merely because execution resumed.
Suppose boot selects firmware named by one record but state named by the other. Could that count as schema-compatible if the schemas happen to match?

The activity checks selection of a firmware-state *pair*, not independent component selection. The selected firmware and state need to be the pair identified by the qualifying record and assessed together for compatibility. An apparent schema match between independently chosen components would not establish that boot selected the newest qualifying pair.
What if neither record is CRC-valid after an injected reset?

Do not invent a qualifying pair or call the check a pass. Record that neither record met the stated CRC-validity condition at that interruption point, and examine what boot actually did. That case would be important to interpreting whether the proposed two-record recovery mechanism can always leave a selectable compatible pair. The activity does not supply a separate fallback rule for it.
Can we use these reset injections to claim that every possible update-time reset has been handled?

The run will test the byte-boundary interruption points it actually exercises across both records. Covering those points is informative, but a claim about *any* update-time reset also depends on the completeness of the interruption model and on how the underlying storage behaves if reset occurs during a write. BootCut-512 results, once available, should be stated for the tested points rather than automatically generalized to every possible reset.
Does this activity measure 1-ms control deadlines or actuator latches after reboot?

Not as stated. BootCut-512 injects byte-boundary resets across the commit records and checks selection of the newest CRC-valid, schema-compatible firmware-state pair. It does not specify measurements of 1-ms deadlines, physical latch intervals, or command continuity. Those properties should not be inferred from a compatible boot selection.
How would you write a concise run instruction that makes the verification criterion unambiguous?

Run BootCut-512 with resets injected at byte boundaries across both commit records. For each reset, determine which recorded firmware-state pairs are CRC-valid and schema-compatible, identify the newest qualifying pair under the defined ordering rule, and check that boot selects that complete pair. Record the outcome rather than presuming recovery succeeds.
BootCut-512 selected the newest fully committed, CRC-valid, schema-compatible firmware-state pair in all 512 resets. Zero mixed pairs booted. How should I report that result?

You can state it directly: ‘In all 512 BootCut-512 resets, boot selected the newest fully committed, CRC-valid, schema-compatible firmware-state pair; zero mixed firmware-state pairs booted.’ This reports the observed selection and pairing outcomes without converting the tested resets into a guarantee about every possible reset.
Should I say ‘512/512’ or just ‘all resets’?

‘512/512’ makes the scope explicit. ‘All resets’ is accurate if you clearly mean all 512 resets in BootCut-512, but without that qualification it could sound like a claim about any update-time reset. You could write: ‘BootCut-512 selected the qualifying pair in 512/512 tested resets, with zero mixed pairs booted.’
What does ‘newest’ mean in that finding?

It means newest among pairs that met *all* the stated conditions: fully committed, CRC-valid, and schema-compatible. The finding does not say boot simply chose the largest visible version number or the most recently touched record regardless of its validity. It says the pair selected in each of the 512 resets was the newest qualifying one.
Why keep ‘fully committed’ if the record already passed a CRC check?

Because they express distinct qualifications. CRC validity concerns the record’s integrity under its check; full commitment concerns whether the pair had completed the commitment required for selection. The reported outcome includes both. Omitting ‘fully committed’ could misleadingly suggest that any CRC-valid candidate was eligible to boot.
And what does schema-compatible add to the description?

It says the selected firmware and state were compatible under the relevant schema relationship, rather than merely present or referenced by a readable record. Full commitment and CRC validity do not, by themselves, describe the firmware-state compatibility finding. All three qualifications belong in the result.
If boot chose a complete pair, isn't ‘zero mixed pairs booted’ redundant?

It is related but worth stating as its own observation. The first finding describes *which* eligible pair boot selected in each reset: the newest one. ‘Zero mixed pairs booted’ explicitly describes the absence of boots combining components from different pairs. Keeping both makes the selection criterion and the pairing outcome visible.
Can I write that there were zero corrupted records?

No. The result says which pair boot selected and that no mixed pair booted; it does not report a count of corrupted or CRC-invalid records. Boot could select a qualifying pair without that implying that every record was intact. Preserve the stated outcome instead of inferring an unreported condition of both records.
Does this mean the candidate pair always booted?

Not necessarily. The result identifies the selected pair by its eligibility and recency, not by saying it was always the candidate or always the previously committed pair. Which particular pair qualified as newest could depend on the reset point. No per-reset breakdown of pair identities is given here.
Could I claim that boot always chose the newest firmware image?

That would leave out the central pairing condition. The observed choice was the newest *fully committed, CRC-valid, schema-compatible firmware-state pair*. Selecting an image on its own is not equivalent to selecting that complete pair, and ‘newest firmware image’ could include one whose associated state was not eligible.
What exactly is ruled out by ‘zero mixed pairs booted’?

Within the 512 observed boots, none booted with firmware from one pair combined with state from another. The statement is about pairs that actually booted in this run. It is not a separate observation about every intermediate value a commit record might have held before boot made its selection.
Does zero mixed pairs also say there were no resets that failed to boot?

The result reports that boot selected the qualifying pair in all 512 resets, so each of those tested resets had a reported successful pair selection. ‘Zero mixed pairs’ alone would not establish that; the all-512 selection result supplies that information. Neither statement provides further details about behavior after selection.
Can the result establish that the firmware met the 1 ms control deadline after each boot?

No. BootCut-512 reports recovery selection for 512 resets and zero mixed pairs booted. It does not report control timing after reboot, physical latch intervals, or actuator-command continuity. Pair compatibility and real-time behavior are different observations.
Could it establish that there were no skipped or duplicated actuator commands during the resets?

No. A reset interrupts execution, and this result concerns which firmware-state pair boot selected afterward. It contains no measurement of actuator commands during a reset or of their sequence after recovery. ‘Zero mixed pairs booted’ should not be turned into ‘zero skipped or duplicated actuator commands.’
How much can I say about resets interrupting the commit records?

You can identify BootCut-512 as the byte-boundary reset test across both commit records and report its outcome for all 512 tested resets. The evidence says selection succeeded under those tested interruptions. It does not say how many resets affected each individual record or what contents were visible at each interruption, so avoid supplying a breakdown that has not been reported.
Does 512/512 make this a guarantee for any update-time reset?

No. It establishes what BootCut-512 observed at its 512 tested resets. A claim covering *any* update-time reset would also require confidence that the tested interruption points and the underlying persistence behavior account for every reachable update-time state. That broader coverage is not itself stated by the result.
Is it fair to say this supports the idea of dual CRC-protected records and immutable A/B manifests?

Yes, in the bounded sense that the observed boot selections are consistent with the intended recovery behavior of that approach at the tested reset points. Report the concrete outcome—newest fully committed, CRC-valid, schema-compatible pair in all 512 resets, with zero mixed boots—rather than replacing it with an unconditional assertion that the record and manifest design cannot fail under any interruption.
Can I call the test a failure-free firmware update?

That would broaden the result beyond what was measured. BootCut-512 observed recovery pair selection after its reset injections. It does not, in this finding, assess the entire update process, migration-rejection behavior, or 1 ms actuator deadlines. ‘No incorrect pair selections or mixed-pair boots in the 512 tested resets’ stays closer to the observation.
What if a reader assumes CRC-valid means schema-compatible?

Keep both adjectives in the finding and, if necessary, explain their different roles. CRC-valid concerns the checked integrity of the record; schema-compatible concerns the firmware-state pairing. The result requires both, along with full commitment, before calling a pair eligible for selection.
Does the evidence identify the specific A or B slot chosen after every reset?

No slot-by-slot choices are included in this finding. It reports that the selected pair was the newest qualifying one in every one of 512 resets and that no mixed pair booted. Avoid asserting an A-versus-B count or a particular choice at a particular boundary without the underlying per-reset information.
Could I state the result as ‘all commit records remained valid after reset’?

No. Boot’s selection of a CRC-valid pair does not mean both commit records remained valid after each reset. The finding describes the pair that was selected, not the status of every record. This distinction matters when characterizing a test involving interruptions across both records.
How would you separate the result from its interpretation in two sentences?

‘BootCut-512 selected the newest fully committed, CRC-valid, schema-compatible firmware-state pair in all 512 tested resets, and zero mixed pairs booted. This is evidence of compatible pair selection at those tested reset points, not by itself a universal recovery guarantee or a measurement of actuator timing.’
Give me the shortest accurate results-line version.
BootCut-512: 512/512 resets selected the newest fully committed, CRC-valid, schema-compatible firmware-state pair; zero mixed pairs booted.

For migrating live control state, I propose tick-stamped copy-on-write snapshots, 50-µs background migration slices, and replaying intervening state deltas before cutover. How do those pieces fit together?

The tick stamp identifies the point in the control sequence represented by a snapshot. Copy-on-write lets the active firmware-state pair continue changing its live state while the snapshot remains a stable basis for preparing candidate state. The proposed 50-µs background slices divide migration work into small portions rather than doing it all at the cutover boundary. Before cutover, replay the state changes made since the snapshot so the candidate state represents a coherent, current handoff point.

That is a proposed way to prepare state while control continues, not evidence yet that its scheduling, delta capture, or final replay will meet every 1 ms deadline.
Why stamp the snapshot with a tick rather than just record that it was taken at some time?

A tick stamp relates the snapshot to the control sequence whose state changes must be accounted for. It gives a reference for deciding which later state deltas belong in the catch-up replay and where that replay should stop for a proposed cutover. A wall-clock timestamp alone might not say which control tick's changes the snapshot includes.

The stamp has to have a defined meaning: for example, whether it identifies a state before or after the associated tick. The proposal does not choose that convention, but consistency between snapshotting, delta capture, and cutover depends on it.
What does copy-on-write actually protect while the active state keeps evolving?

It protects the snapshot's view from being silently changed by later writes to the active state. Migration can then work from a stable starting point while ongoing control still updates the live state. Without that separation, a migration slice might read a mixture of state from different ticks and call it one snapshot.

Copy-on-write is not, by itself, a guarantee that acquiring the snapshot is atomic at the chosen tick, that all subsequent changes are recorded, or that its overhead fits a 1 ms control deadline. Those properties still need to be established.
Does taking a snapshot mean pausing actuator control for one tick?

Not under the intended uninterrupted-update requirement. A tick-stamped snapshot has to be obtained without missing the 1 ms control deadline or skipping that tick's actuator command. The proposal's purpose is to allow control to continue while migration proceeds; it does not authorize a pause followed by catch-up commands.
How should I interpret a 50-µs background migration slice?

It describes a unit of migration work allotted 50 µs in the background. The point is to keep migration from occupying an unbounded uninterrupted stretch of control-path time. But a 50-µs slice is not automatically harmless: its scheduling, resource contention, and any work needed to stop it or resume control also matter to the 1 ms deadline.

The proposal does not state how many slices there are, when they run, or how long the total migration takes. It should not be read as a measured 50-µs cost for the entire update.
Could I run one 50-µs slice whenever the controller has time and assume the deadline is protected?

The background placement helps only if the work, including its interference with the control loop, actually leaves enough time for every required 1 ms tick. Calling a slice ‘background’ does not prove it cannot block the scheduler, the actuator path, or access to live state. The proposal needs an accounting of those effects rather than an assumption based on the slice's name.
What are the intervening state deltas supposed to represent?

They represent relevant changes to live state after the tick-stamped snapshot and before the chosen cutover state. Their purpose is to bring the candidate's migrated state forward from its snapshot basis while control keeps running. The proposal does not specify a delta format, but replay has to preserve the meaning and ordering of changes needed for a coherent candidate state.
Does replaying deltas mean rerunning earlier actuator ticks or resending their commands?

No. This is replay of *state changes into the candidate state*, not replay of the controller's actuator-command sequence. Previously served ticks must not be commanded again. The active pair continues meeting current control obligations while the candidate catches up internally, and only a valid cutover gives the candidate authority for its assigned future ticks.
Suppose the snapshot is stamped at tick N. Which deltas should be replayed?

That depends on what the stamp says the snapshot includes. If it denotes a coherent state after tick N, catch-up must account for relevant changes after that state and through the state selected for cutover. If it denotes a state before N, then changes during N also have to be accounted for. Either convention can be reasoned about, but the snapshot and replay cannot disagree about it; otherwise a change could be included twice or omitted.

Here N is just an illustrative tick label, not a statement about a particular implementation.
Why is the ordering of state deltas important?

A later state change may depend on an earlier one. Applying changes out of order, or applying one twice, could leave the candidate state different from the state that ongoing control produced. The replay rule needs to preserve whatever dependencies the actual state transitions have. A collection of deltas with the right tick stamps is not necessarily sufficient if their meaning or order is ambiguous.
Could we just replay the deltas captured so far and switch immediately?

Only if ‘so far’ includes every change the candidate must reflect at the defined cutover boundary. While replay is running, the active state may keep changing and create additional deltas. The design needs a coherent point at which the replayed state and the handoff agree; otherwise the candidate could start with a state that is already behind the active pair's final assigned tick.

The proposal says to replay intervening deltas *before cutover*. It does not specify a method for closing the final catch-up interval, so that boundary still needs a precise definition.
Is there a risk that the deltas arrive faster than the 50-µs slices can migrate and replay them?

That is a condition to examine. If the candidate cannot catch up with changes made by ongoing control, its backlog may remain nonzero at every proposed cutover boundary. The proposal does not give state-change rates, migration work, or the number of available slices, so it cannot establish that catch-up completes. Cutover should not be assumed safe merely because migration has made progress.
Does the 50-µs limit also apply to final delta replay right before switching?

The proposal explicitly calls for 50-µs *background migration slices* and replay of intervening deltas before cutover. It does not specify a separate time bound for final replay or say that all final work fits in a single slice. Whatever work remains on the control path at the boundary must still fit the 1 ms deadline. It would be misleading to infer that the background slice size alone bounds the final handoff.
How does this interact with a state-schema change? Are old-state deltas necessarily valid updates to new-state fields?

No. Catch-up must account for the meaning of changes under the candidate schema, not merely copy changes as if old and new representations were identical. Whether a delta can be transformed or applied depends on the migration's compatibility rules. The proposal does not name schema fields or a transformation, so it cannot assume every delta replays successfully. If the resulting candidate state is incompatible, it must not become the active firmware-state pair.
Would checking the migrated snapshot for compatibility be enough before cutover?

Not necessarily. The state that matters at cutover is the migrated snapshot *after* all required intervening deltas have been accounted for. A snapshot might pass a check while a later change cannot be represented correctly in the candidate schema, or while replay leaves an invalid state. Compatibility must cover the candidate state that would actually be selected, without partly replacing the active pair if validation fails.
Can a delta be skipped if it seems irrelevant to actuator output?

Not just on that description. A change might affect later control behavior or a condition the candidate firmware expects, even if it does not change the immediate actuator value. The replay needs a defined rule for which changes are relevant to a coherent migrated state. The proposal supplies no state schema or dependency analysis that would justify discarding a particular delta.
If copy-on-write and delta capture both observe the same change, could it be applied twice?

That is exactly why the tick stamp and the snapshot boundary need precise semantics. Each change must be accounted for once in the candidate state: either already represented in the snapshot being migrated or included in the intervening deltas to replay. The proposal aims to make that separation possible, but it does not prove that a particular capture and replay implementation has excluded overlap or omissions.
What must remain true about actuator commands during all of this background work?

The active control path must keep meeting its 1 ms deadlines and issuing the required actuator commands without duplication or skips throughout an uninterrupted update. Snapshotting, copy-on-write bookkeeping, 50-µs migration slices, and delta recording can all affect that path, so each must be included in the timing and command-consistency argument. State replay in the candidate must never be mistaken for authorization to issue past actuator commands.
Does this proposal tell us what happens if the controller resets while a shadow snapshot is being migrated?

It does not establish reset recovery by itself. A partial shadow migration or an unfinished delta replay should not be mistaken for a committed, compatible firmware-state pair. After any update-time reset, recovery still needs to select a compatible pair under the update's commitment rule. Tick stamps and 50-µs slices address preparation and catch-up during live control; they do not alone define a recoverable commit.
How would I phrase the proposed cutover condition without claiming the candidate is already ready?

You could say: ‘Permit cutover only after a tick-stamped copy-on-write snapshot has been migrated, all state deltas intervening up to a coherent handoff boundary have been replayed, and the resulting candidate firmware-state pair is validated as compatible; the remaining handoff work must still meet the 1 ms deadline.’ That states what readiness would require, not that the work has finished or passed validation.
What's the concise version of the whole proposal?

Use tick-stamped copy-on-write snapshots to give migration a stable starting state, perform migration in 50-µs background slices while control continues, and replay all intervening state deltas into the candidate before a coherent cutover. Validate the resulting firmware-state pair and preserve the 1 ms deadline and actuator-command sequence throughout; the proposed mechanisms still need timing and consistency verification.
How can delta replay reach a consistent tick boundary while control ticks keep modifying the snapshot?

First distinguish the snapshot from live state. With the proposed copy-on-write snapshot, control ticks keep modifying *live* state; the snapshot must remain a stable view identified by its tick stamp. The candidate starts from that view and replays the intervening changes. The difficult part is closing the interval between the last delta replayed and the tick at which the candidate takes over.

A consistent handoff needs a clearly defined final tick owned by the current pair. The candidate must incorporate all relevant changes through that tick, and none from a later tick assigned to the candidate. Control can continue while preparation proceeds, but cutover cannot occur merely because replay has caught up to an earlier point.
So does replay have to catch up to the live state at every instant?

No. It can temporarily lag while the active pair continues control. It needs to reach a *defined tick boundary* at which the candidate state is coherent and ready to become authoritative. That is different from continuously matching a moving live state at every instant. The design must show that it can reach such a boundary without delaying a required 1 ms tick.
If a new delta is recorded while an earlier one is being replayed, does that invalidate the work already done?

Not necessarily. The earlier replay can remain valid if deltas have a well-defined order and the new delta is retained for subsequent replay. What would invalidate the handoff is selecting the candidate after replaying an incomplete or ambiguous set of changes. The candidate must reflect every relevant change through its chosen handoff tick, exactly once, in the order required by the state transitions.
Could we just say ‘replay until there are no deltas left’?

That is not a sufficient boundary rule while control keeps producing deltas. The backlog might briefly reach zero and then grow again, or a change might be in progress when the empty check occurs. The rule needs to identify *which ticks’ changes* are included and ensure no change belonging to the current pair’s final assigned tick can appear after the candidate is treated as ready for that boundary.
What would a tick stamp need to tell the replayer?

It needs an unambiguous inclusion convention: whether the snapshot represents state before or after its named tick. Deltas then need to be ordered relative to that point, and the final handoff needs an equally clear endpoint. Without those meanings, a change at either edge could be replayed twice or omitted. The proposal names tick stamps but does not specify their representation or convention.
Can you illustrate the endpoint without prescribing a particular delta-log implementation?

Suppose the current pair owns tick N and the candidate is intended to own tick N+1. The candidate state for that handoff must reflect the relevant changes through N. Changes belonging to N must not be left pending, while work belonging to N+1 must not be replayed as though the current pair had performed it. Once that state is ready and compatible, pair selection can be considered at the boundary, subject to the deadline and actuator-ownership conditions.

N is just an illustrative tick label; this does not prescribe how changes are captured or when a specific controller can complete replay.
What if the final tick writes state after its actuator command has been issued?

Then command issuance alone would not establish that the final tick’s state is complete. The handoff definition must account for all state changes attributed to that tick, in whatever order the control path actually performs them. A candidate built from an earlier partial view would not necessarily be coherent just because the actuator command for the tick has an issued ID.
Could the current pair keep running the next tick while we finish replay through N?

It could continue owning ticks if cutover is deferred. But then a proposed handoff after a later tick requires accounting for the changes from that later tick too. The endpoint cannot remain N while the active pair performs further state-changing ticks and the candidate is selected as though it were current. Continued control is required; the handoff boundary can move, but its associated state must move with it.
Does this mean migration can never finish because the boundary keeps moving?

Not necessarily. Background migration can complete most of the work from the stable snapshot, leaving a smaller set of intervening deltas to handle near a prospective boundary. Whether that remaining work can be brought to a coherent endpoint depends on how fast relevant changes accumulate, how quickly they can be replayed, and how the final boundary is coordinated. The proposal supplies no rates or bounds that would prove catch-up is possible in every case.
Could we briefly stop control to make the backlog stay at zero?

Not if stopping control causes an uninterrupted update to miss a 1 ms control deadline or skip an actuator command. A consistent endpoint must be achieved within the control timing constraints. It would be reasonable to ask whether final coordination can fit between assigned ticks, but its feasibility has to be demonstrated rather than assumed from the word ‘briefly.’
Do the 50-µs background slices solve that final coordination problem?

They limit the proposed units of background migration work; they do not, by themselves, bound the amount of final delta replay or coordination needed at the handoff. A design has to account for the final catch-up cost and any interference from copy-on-write and delta capture as well as the slices themselves. All uninterrupted 1 ms control deadlines remain in force.
What prevents a change from being recorded too late, after the replayer has declared the state ready?

The readiness condition needs a boundary with a reliable answer to whether every change through the current pair’s final tick is represented. If changes can still be attributed to that tick after readiness is declared, the candidate is not demonstrably current at that boundary. There are different possible coordination mechanisms, but the proposal does not select one; the necessary property is that no required delta can fall between the final replay decision and the pair handoff unnoticed.
Would a simple count of pending deltas prove that property?

No. A count of zero says something about the backlog at the moment it was read. It does not establish that capture of the final tick is complete, that an in-progress change has been recorded, or that the replayed changes produced compatible candidate state. A usable cutover condition needs to relate completed tick ownership, delta inclusion, and validation of the state actually selected.
How does replay account for schema changes if a delta describes the old firmware’s state?

The candidate must reflect the *meaning* of the intervening change under its own schema. Simply applying an old-state representation to a new-state representation could be invalid. The migration and delta-replay rules must be compatible, and the resulting candidate state must be validated before it is selected. The question gives no particular schema or delta format, so no universal transformation can be assumed.
If replay of one delta is incompatible, should we switch anyway because the earlier snapshot migration succeeded?

No. The candidate would not have a validated, coherent state at the intended handoff point. A snapshot migration that initially passes does not override a later incompatibility in the state that would actually be selected. The incompatible candidate must not be partially activated or committed; the active compatible pair can continue handling its assigned ticks while the candidate is rejected.
Does replaying a state delta ever entitle the candidate to issue the actuator command from that old tick?

No. Replaying state changes is internal preparation of the candidate, not replay of actuator commands. The current pair has command ownership for its assigned ticks. If the candidate is selected at a coherent boundary, it takes ownership only of ticks assigned after that boundary. This separation prevents state catch-up from becoming an accidental command replay.
What if a reset occurs after replay has caught up but before the candidate pair is committed?

Catch-up does not itself make a firmware-state pair recoverably committed. After an update-time reset, boot still has to select a compatible pair established by the commitment rule; an uncommitted shadow candidate must not be mistaken for it. The tick-stamped snapshot and replay address live-state coherence before cutover, not the persistent proof that a pair was committed.
What observations would tell us that a particular proposed handoff boundary is coherent?

For that boundary, establish which tick was last assigned to the current pair; that its relevant state changes were captured; that each delta since the snapshot through that tick was applied to the candidate exactly once in the required order; and that the resulting candidate firmware-state pair passed compatibility checks. Separately establish that switching at the boundary preserves the 1 ms control deadline and exactly one actuator command for each required tick. None of those outcomes follows merely from a small backlog.
So what is the central answer to the moving-target problem?

Do not try to make replay match a continuously moving state indefinitely. Use the tick stamps to define a precise final tick for the current pair, account for all relevant deltas through that tick, and permit cutover only when the candidate state for that boundary is coherent and compatible. If that cannot be established within the 1 ms timing and actuator-command constraints, leave the current pair in control and defer the handoff. How the final delta interval is closed remains an implementation question, not an observed success.

To address the moving-target problem, let's replay the SwapStress-10k writes with tick-sealed delta logs and 50-µs slices. We should verify backlog clearance and cutover-state equality. How should I describe that activity?

Describe it as a replay and verification activity: replay the SwapStress-10k writes while using tick-sealed delta logs and 50-µs migration slices; at each proposed cutover boundary, check that the required delta backlog has cleared and that the candidate’s cutover state equals the expected state for that boundary. Those are checks to perform, not results already observed.
What does ‘tick-sealed’ contribute to the delta log?

A seal is meant to establish that the changes belonging to a particular tick are complete in the log. That gives replay a definite endpoint: it can account for all required changes through a sealed tick rather than treating a momentarily empty backlog as proof that no more changes from that tick can arrive. The activity does not specify how sealing is implemented or how its completeness is enforced.
Would it be enough for replay to see an empty queue before cutover?

Not by itself. An empty queue could precede the recording of a change from a tick still in progress. Backlog clearance must be assessed relative to a sealed tick that defines the proposed handoff state. The relevant question is whether every required delta through that tick has been applied, with none still pending or arriving later as part of that tick.
Does a sealed tick mean the active controller has stopped producing new deltas?

No. Control may continue into later ticks and produce later deltas. Sealing makes the log for one identified tick complete; it does not freeze live control state indefinitely. A candidate prepared for cutover after that tick needs to reflect the state through it. If cutover is deferred and the active pair executes additional ticks, their relevant changes must be accounted for at the later boundary.
How do the 50-µs slices relate to the replay?

They are the proposed work units for doing migration and catch-up without making that work one unbounded operation. The replay should exercise the workload while work is divided into 50-µs slices and then assess whether the deltas can be cleared at a coherent boundary. The slice duration alone does not prove that the backlog will clear, that final coordination fits, or that the controller meets every 1 ms deadline.
Can I assume that one 50-µs slice is enough to process each tick’s deltas?

No. The activity gives a slice size, not the number of deltas per tick or the work needed to migrate and replay them. Backlog clearance is one of the things to verify. Assuming it in advance would turn the intended observation into a premise.
What does ‘replay the SwapStress-10k writes’ mean in this activity?

It identifies the writes from SwapStress-10k as the workload being replayed while exercising tick-sealed logging and sliced migration. It does not mean replaying actuator commands or rerunning past physical latch events. The state-write workload is used to examine whether the candidate state can be brought up to the selected tick boundary.
Should I say the replay reproduces exactly the same control timing as SwapStress-10k?

No. Using its writes identifies the workload input; it does not establish identical timing or outcomes in this activity. The checks stated here concern backlog clearance and cutover-state equality under tick-sealed delta logging and 50-µs slices. If timing is measured, it should be reported as its own observation rather than inferred from the workload source.
What is the backlog whose clearance we're checking?

It is the set of relevant state changes after the snapshot that still need to be incorporated into the candidate state for the proposed cutover tick. A clear backlog means none of the required deltas through that sealed boundary remain unapplied. It does not require the absence of deltas from later ticks that the active pair may already be handling.
If the backlog reaches zero between ticks, can we record that as success?

Record what happened, but do not call it verified cutover readiness solely on that basis. The check needs an identified sealed endpoint, confirmation that replay includes the required deltas through it, and a comparison of the resulting cutover state. A zero backlog at an unqualified instant does not settle whether the candidate matches the state at the boundary where ownership would change.
How should the cutover-state equality check handle a changed state schema?

It should compare the state the candidate would use at the proposed cutover with the expected result of migrating and replaying changes through that same tick. Equality must be defined in terms appropriate to the two schemas; raw byte equality between differently represented states might not express the intended condition. The activity does not specify the schemas or the comparison rule, so those must be defined before the check can be interpreted.
Do we need to compare against a state from the exact tick chosen for cutover?

Yes. A candidate that matches an earlier tick may still be behind by changes made during the current pair’s final assigned tick. The comparison must use a coherent reference for the proposed cutover boundary and the candidate after replay through that same boundary. Otherwise, a mismatch could reflect comparing different ticks, or an apparent match could hide a missing final delta.
Could matching state at the end of the replay establish that each delta was applied exactly once?

A matching cutover state is the specified outcome to verify, but it does not necessarily reveal how every individual delta was handled. Depending on the state changes, an omission and another error could conceivably produce a matching comparison. Tick-sealed log coverage and backlog clearance should therefore be interpreted alongside cutover-state equality, rather than treating one end-state comparison as a full trace of every replay operation.
What if the log for the intended final tick has not yet been sealed?

Then replay does not yet have a confirmed complete set of changes for that tick, so the activity cannot establish clearance through that boundary. It may continue work on earlier sealed ticks, but it should not mark the candidate’s state equal to a final cutover state before the relevant boundary is defined and complete. That is a condition for interpreting the check, not an assertion that it occurred.
If cutover moves to a later tick, can we keep the previous equality result?

Only as a result about the earlier boundary. A later cutover requires accounting for changes through the later sealed tick and comparing the candidate with the state expected there. Equality at an earlier tick does not automatically persist while active control continues to write state.
What if the delta backlog never clears while the writes are being replayed?

That would mean the clearance check has not been met for the proposed boundaries examined; it should be reported as such rather than claiming cutover-state readiness. The activity supplies no write rate, processing rate, or observed result, so it does not establish whether this will occur. Continuing to execute 50-µs slices is not equivalent to catching up.
And if the backlog clears but the candidate's cutover state differs from the expected state?

Report the two checks separately: the required logged work appears cleared for the chosen boundary, but cutover-state equality is not established. An empty backlog cannot validate a candidate state that differs from the reference. The activity is intended to detect both kinds of problem without assuming one check implies the other.
Would state equality alone show the candidate firmware can interpret the migrated state?

Not necessarily. Cutover-state equality addresses consistency of the state reached by replay with the expected state at the boundary. Schema compatibility for the candidate firmware is a distinct condition. The activity specified here verifies backlog clearance and cutover-state equality; it should not be reported as an additional compatibility-validation result unless that is separately established.
Does this replay check that actuator commands remain uninterrupted?

Not by its stated verification criteria. Replaying state writes must not itself replay actuator commands, and any real cutover still has to meet the 1 ms deadline and command-consistency requirements. But backlog clearance and cutover-state equality alone do not demonstrate actuator latch timing or exactly-once command delivery. Keep the stated activity’s conclusions limited to the state-catch-up question.
How can I phrase the checks so ‘equality’ doesn't imply that the active state stopped changing?

Tie equality to a named sealed tick: compare the candidate state after replay through that tick with the expected state at that tick’s cutover boundary. Live control may continue afterward; the comparison says whether the two views agree at the selected boundary, not whether state remains fixed for subsequent ticks.
What's the concise run instruction?

Replay the SwapStress-10k writes using tick-sealed delta logs and 50-µs migration slices. For each proposed cutover boundary examined, verify that all required deltas through the sealed tick have cleared and that the replayed candidate state equals the expected cutover state for that tick. Record the findings without presuming either check passes.
The SwapStress-10k write replay produced 72 µs/tick of delta work. With 50-µs slices, it accrued a 220 ms backlog across 10,000 ticks. How should I report that?

Report the observation directly: ‘In the SwapStress-10k replay, delta work was 72 µs/tick, and processing it in 50-µs slices accrued a 220 ms backlog across 10,000 ticks.’ Keep the work rate, slice size, backlog, and tick count attached to the replay. This is an observed catch-up problem, not a measurement of actuator timing or cutover-state equality.
Do the numbers explain the size of the backlog?

Their arithmetic is consistent: 72 µs minus 50 µs is 22 µs per tick, and 22 µs/tick across 10,000 ticks is 220,000 µs, or 220 ms. That is a useful way to explain the reported accumulation. It should not be used to invent a detailed scheduling trace or a count of slices per tick that the finding does not state.
Is 220 ms the delay experienced by one control tick?

No. The 220 ms is the backlog accrued across 10,000 ticks, expressed as an amount of pending delta work. It is not reported as the latency of one tick, one actuator latch, or one firmware-state-pair swap. Likewise, 72 µs/tick describes the delta work produced per tick in this replay; it is not a measured control-tick execution time.
Can I conclude that the backlog cleared before cutover?

No. The reported observation is that a 220 ms backlog accrued, not that it cleared. To claim clearance at a proposed cutover boundary, the required deltas through that boundary would have to be accounted for. This finding does not report such a boundary or a subsequent clearance observation.
What does the backlog mean for a candidate state built from a snapshot?

It means delta work remained to bring the candidate forward from its snapshot basis under the measured replay conditions. A candidate cannot be declared current at a cutover boundary merely because some migration slices have completed; the relevant changes through that boundary still need to be incorporated. The reported backlog does not identify a particular candidate state or show whether it equaled an expected cutover state.
Should I say the cutover-state equality check failed?

Not from this finding alone. It reports a rate of 72 µs/tick and an accumulated 220 ms backlog with 50-µs slices across 10,000 ticks. It does not report a comparison of the replayed candidate state with an expected cutover state. You can say that backlog clearance was not shown by these measurements; do not add an equality result that was not reported.
Would an eventual matching state make the 220 ms backlog irrelevant?

An eventual comparison would answer a question about the state at the boundary it examines. It would not change the fact that the measured replay accrued 220 ms of backlog over 10,000 ticks. The two observations should remain distinct: whether work accumulates under these slices, and whether a candidate state at some defined boundary matches its expected state. No eventual matching result is supplied here.
Does 72 µs/tick mean every individual tick produced exactly 72 µs of work?

The finding states 72 µs/tick of delta work for the replay. It does not provide a per-tick distribution or say that every tick produced an identical amount. Report the stated rate without turning it into an unreported claim about each individual tick.
Are the 50-µs slices a measured maximum execution time?

The finding identifies the migration slices as 50 µs. It does not give a distribution of actual slice execution times or establish a worst-case bound for all slice-related interference. Here, the important reported outcome is that using those slices coincided with a 220 ms backlog across the 10,000 ticks.
Can I say the replay missed 1-ms deadlines because the backlog grew?

No. Backlog growth concerns outstanding delta-replay work; a missed 1 ms control deadline is a separate timing observation. The finding gives no deadline-miss count, actuator-latch interval, or duplicated-command observation. A backlog may affect when a candidate is ready for cutover, but its size alone does not establish that an active control tick ran late.
Does the backlog imply that past actuator commands need to be replayed to catch up?

No. The backlog is delta work for candidate *state*. Processing it must not resend actuator commands from ticks the active pair has already served. State catch-up and actuator-command progression are different sequences, and this result measures only the former.
What is the specific concern for reaching a consistent tick boundary?

A consistent cutover state must include the relevant deltas through its designated final tick. In this replay, the stated 50-µs slices accrued pending work rather than demonstrating clearance across the 10,000 ticks. Thus the result raises a concrete catch-up concern for a proposed boundary under these measured conditions; it does not establish whether another boundary or processing arrangement could satisfy the requirement.
Would simply choosing a later tick eliminate the observed backlog?

Not automatically. If control continues producing relevant changes, a later handoff boundary also requires accounting for those later changes. The replay’s measured accumulation cannot be declared cleared merely by moving the boundary. Whether a later boundary can be reached coherently would require its own backlog-clearance observation.
Should the report say the 50-µs sliced migration approach can never work?

No. The result is specific to the SwapStress-10k writes replayed under the stated conditions: 72 µs/tick of delta work and 220 ms of backlog across 10,000 ticks with 50-µs slices. It shows that this measured replay did not demonstrate a cleared backlog. It does not give grounds for a universal claim about every workload or every way slices might be scheduled.
What is the shortest accurate findings line?
SwapStress-10k write replay produced 72 µs/tick of delta work; 50-µs migration slices accrued a 220 ms backlog across 10,000 ticks.
Let's reject fixed 50-µs delta replay: peak-load writes generate 72 µs/tick of delta work, preventing convergence before cutover. How should I state the decision?

‘Reject fixed 50-µs delta replay for cutover. Peak-load writes generate 72 µs/tick of delta work, so that fixed replay allocation cannot converge before cutover.’ This states both the decision and its reason, without implying that the active control loop missed a deadline.
What exactly does ‘converge’ mean in this decision?

It means bringing the candidate state up to the coherent tick boundary needed for cutover: the relevant changes through that boundary must have been replayed rather than remaining pending. The stated reason is that peak-load writes generate 72 µs/tick of delta work while replay is fixed at 50 µs. Under that arrangement, work accumulates instead of being cleared before cutover.
Is the comparison between 50 µs and the full 1 ms tick?

No. The decisive comparison here is between 50 µs of fixed delta replay and 72 µs/tick of delta work generated by peak-load writes. The 1 ms tick remains the control period, but the rejection is based on replay failing to catch up before cutover, not on a finding that a control tick exceeded 1 ms.
Can you express the shortfall numerically?

The stated generation rate exceeds the fixed replay allocation by 22 µs per tick: 72 µs/tick minus 50 µs/tick. That explains why the candidate cannot catch up under the fixed arrangement. It does not quantify actuator timing or specify how another replay allocation would affect control.
Does the decision reject using delta replay at all?

No. Its scope is *fixed 50-µs delta replay* under the stated peak-load writes. It does not rule out delta replay with a different way of meeting the catch-up requirement. Nor does it select such an alternative; this decision only says the specified fixed allocation prevents convergence before cutover.
Should I say the cutover itself was rejected?

Be narrower: the rejected element is the fixed 50-µs delta-replay approach to preparing state for cutover. A cutover needs a coherent candidate state, and this arrangement does not converge before that boundary under peak-load writes. The decision does not say that firmware-state-pair cutover in general is impossible.
Could we still cut over if some deltas remain, since the candidate has already migrated most of the state?

That would not satisfy the convergence condition expressed in this decision. The candidate needs the relevant intervening changes through its intended handoff tick; ‘most of the state’ is not a substitute for a coherent cutover state. Rejecting the fixed replay allocation avoids treating an unfinished catch-up as ready merely because substantial work has been done.
What if we simply wait for a later tick before switching?

Moving the boundary later does not, by itself, resolve a replay allocation that is below the rate at which peak-load writes generate delta work. Later ticks can add more work that must be included for a later cutover state. The decision’s reason is precisely that the fixed 50-µs arrangement does not converge before cutover under the stated rate; waiting alone should not be presented as a demonstrated solution.
Does ‘72 µs/tick’ say every individual peak-load tick generated exactly that amount?

The decision states that peak-load writes generate 72 µs/tick of delta work. It does not give an individual-tick distribution or require interpreting each tick as identical. Retain the reported rate when explaining why a fixed 50-µs replay allocation is insufficient.
Does this finding tell us whether the state migration was schema-incompatible?

No. Failure to converge is about outstanding delta work before cutover, not a reported schema-validation failure. A candidate might have a valid migration of its snapshot while still lacking the intervening changes required for the cutover state. This decision rejects the fixed replay arrangement for that catch-up reason; it does not issue a compatibility verdict on a particular candidate.
And should I describe this as an actuator-command failure?

No. The stated reason concerns the rate of generated delta work and failure to converge before cutover. It does not report a missing or duplicate actuator command or a 1 ms deadline miss. Those are separate control-path properties, and this decision should not be broadened into an unreported actuator outcome.
What is the clearest way to preserve both the scope and the reason in one line?
Reject fixed 50-µs delta replay for cutover because peak-load writes generate 72 µs/tick of delta work, preventing the candidate state from converging before cutover.
My hypothesis is that coalescing repeated field writes will reduce delta-replay work below 50 µs/tick, allowing the sealed-tick backlog to drain before cutover. How should I reason about that?

Separate it into a semantic claim and a capacity claim. Semantically, coalescing must preserve the candidate state that replaying the required writes would produce at the chosen tick boundary. Quantitatively, the resulting replay work must fall below 50 µs/tick under the conditions being considered. Only then does the proposed reduction offer a way for a sealed-tick backlog to drain before cutover. Both claims remain hypotheses until checked.
What does coalescing repeated field writes mean without assuming a particular state schema?

It means identifying multiple recorded writes to the same field and representing their necessary effect with less replay work. In a simple conceptual case, several replacements of a field might leave only the final value relevant to the candidate state at a defined boundary. But that simplification is valid only if intermediate writes carry no effect that the migrated state must retain. The hypothesis names repeated field writes; it does not specify fields, write semantics, or a coalescing algorithm.
If a field is written three times, can I always replay only the third write?

No. That would be safe only if the candidate state at the selected boundary depends on the last value and not on the intermediate changes or their effects elsewhere. A write might affect another part of state, or the order of changes might matter. Coalescing has to be defined against the actual state-transition semantics, not inferred solely from repeated field names.
Does coalescing mean the active controller stops making those writes?

No. Active control can continue updating its live state. The hypothesis concerns reducing the work needed to replay recorded changes into candidate state. It must not silently alter how the controlling firmware behaves or authorize the candidate to issue actuator commands for ticks that have already been served.
Why specify ‘below 50 µs/tick’ rather than ‘50 µs/tick or less’?

The hypothesis explicitly says *below* 50 µs/tick. That strict comparison matters to the proposed backlog-drain reasoning: if work arriving and replay capacity merely balance at 50 µs/tick, an existing backlog would not necessarily shrink. Work below that level could leave capacity to process previously pending work, subject to the actual scheduling and any other costs. The hypothesis does not quantify how far below 50 µs/tick the work would be.
Is getting below 50 µs/tick enough to say the backlog has drained?

Not by itself. It would address the proposed rate comparison, but a backlog that already exists still takes time to clear. The design must observe or establish that all required deltas through a particular sealed tick have actually been incorporated before cutover. A favorable rate is a reason drainage may become possible, not evidence that it has already occurred.
What is the role of the sealed tick in this hypothesis?
