Should I call 40 µs a measured upper bound?

No. Forty microseconds is the budget being set, not a measured worst-case replay cost. The measurement named here is 31 µs/tick from CoalesceReplay-10k. The burst-write test will show how the proposed budget behaves under its tested workload; the plan should not present that outcome as known in advance.
Why test burst writes if we already have a replay-cost measurement?

Bursts probe whether concentrated state writes create replay work or pending deltas that the chosen budget cannot clear in time for a coherent cutover. The cited 31-µs/tick cost motivates selecting 40 µs; it does not establish what happens when writes arrive in bursts. Backlog, state equality, and latch timing give separate views of that question.
Could replay stay within the 40-µs budget while a backlog still grows?

Yes. Staying within a work allowance says how much replay ran, not how much new work arrived or whether previously pending work was cleared. Under burst writes, the backlog check must establish whether all relevant changes through a proposed sealed handoff tick have been processed. The budget cannot serve as a substitute for that observation.
Does a brief backlog after a burst mean the test has failed?

Not necessarily. The activity calls for testing burst-write backlog, not for asserting that backlog is zero at every instant. Its relevance to cutover depends on whether the required work through the chosen boundary clears before the candidate is selected. Report how backlog behaves under the tested bursts and whether it clears for the examined boundary; do not infer readiness from its size at an unrelated moment.
How do we define the backlog at a cutover boundary?

Relate it to the last tick whose state changes must be reflected in the candidate. If that tick’s delta log is sealed, the check can ask whether all relevant changes through it have been incorporated, rather than whether a queue happened to be empty while writes continued. The activity does not prescribe a backlog representation or a particular cutover tick; those must be identified when interpreting the test.
What if the burst ends but later control ticks keep writing state?

Then a later cutover boundary must account for those later ticks too. Clearing work associated with the burst at an earlier tick does not automatically make the candidate current at every subsequent boundary. For each cutover examined, associate the backlog and state comparison with that boundary’s required changes.
Could we avoid a backlog by immediately switching before the burst's changes have been replayed?

That would not demonstrate a coherent cutover state. The candidate must incorporate the relevant changes through the tick assigned to the current pair before taking over. The burst-write test should reveal whether that can be achieved under the proposed replay budget, not redefine pending changes as unnecessary merely to permit a switch.
Why compare candidate state if the backlog check says everything was processed?

Processed work can still produce an incorrect candidate state if coalescing or replay fails to preserve the meaning of the writes. Backlog clearance concerns completion of required work; candidate-state equality concerns its result at cutover. Both need a reference to the same tick boundary, and neither should be inferred from the other.
Does ‘state equality’ mean comparing raw bytes of the active and candidate state?

Not necessarily. If a state-schema change is involved, the representations may differ. Define equality in terms of the state expected for the candidate at the selected cutover boundary, with a comparison appropriate to that schema. The activity names a state-equality test but does not prescribe the fields, representation, or comparison method.
What if candidate state matches after the burst, but it did not match at the intended cutover tick?

Report the boundary actually compared. A later match does not establish equality at an earlier intended cutover, because the candidate and live state may represent different sets of tick changes. If cutover is considered at a later boundary, assess the required backlog and state for that later boundary in their own right.
Why measure actuator latch timing in a replay-budget test?

Replay under burst writes may compete with continuing control for time or resources. Measuring latch timing checks whether applying the 40-µs replay budget coincides with acceptable physical actuator timing. A backlog that clears and a candidate state that matches do not, on their own, establish that the actuator path met its 1 ms control obligations.
Would a low average latch interval be enough?

No. An average could conceal a late latch during a burst or near cutover. Preserve timing observations with enough association to the affected ticks to examine individual timing against the relevant 1 ms deadline. Also distinguish spacing between physical latches from each latch’s timing relative to its assigned tick; those are not automatically the same measurement.
If latch timing is acceptable, can I infer the burst backlog cleared?

No. The controller might continue latching on time while candidate-state replay remains behind. Conversely, the backlog might clear while latch timing suffers. The three requested checks—burst-write backlog, state equality, and latch timing—should be reported independently before drawing any conclusion about a proposed cutover.
Would this activity verify exactly one actuator command per 1-ms tick?

Not solely from the measurements it names. Latch timing concerns when latch events occur; an exactly-once finding also requires establishing how many effective events belong to each tick and whether commands were duplicated or skipped. Do not turn a timing profile into an unreported command-count result. The 1 ms control and actuator-consistency requirements still apply during the activity.
Could the 40-µs budget be increased during a burst if that would clear the backlog faster?

That would change the budget being tested. The stated activity is to set a 40-µs replay budget using the measured 31-µs/tick cost, then test burst-write behavior under that choice. A different allowance might be considered separately, but its effect on backlog and actuator latch timing cannot be assumed from this plan.
If the test shows the budget is insufficient, should the candidate still cut over on schedule?

Not if the necessary state changes through the proposed boundary remain pending or candidate-state equality cannot be established. The test is meant to determine whether the candidate becomes ready under burst writes while latching remains timely. It does not authorize selection of an incomplete candidate state to meet an unstated cutover schedule.
Does this burst-write test also check incompatible-migration rejection or boot after a reset?

Those are not stated checks in this activity. It sets a replay budget and tests backlog, candidate-state equality, and latch timing under burst writes. It does not specify an incompatible migration injection or an update-time reset. Its results should not be described as additional rejection or recovery evidence.
How should I keep the measured value and proposed value straight in a run note?

Use different verbs: ‘CoalesceReplay-10k measured 31 µs/tick of replay cost; set a 40-µs replay budget for the burst-write test.’ Then separately say what the test will observe. This avoids presenting 40 µs as an earlier measured maximum or claiming that 31 µs/tick has already been measured under the new burst-write condition.
Can you give me the complete activity statement in one compact paragraph?

Use CoalesceReplay-10k’s measured 31-µs/tick replay cost to set a 40-µs replay budget. Test it under burst writes by recording the sealed-tick backlog, comparing candidate state with the expected state at each examined cutover boundary, and measuring actuator latch timing against the applicable 1 ms control obligation. Treat backlog clearance, state equality, and timely latching as outcomes to check, not results already established for the burst-write test.
The BurstReplay-40 report records backlog with a 40-µs replay budget, candidate-state comparisons, and physical latch intervals under burst-write traces. How should I describe the report itself?

Describe its recorded contents and condition: ‘The BurstReplay-40 report contains 40-µs replay-budget backlog records, candidate-state comparisons, and physical actuator latch intervals under burst-write traces.’ That identifies what a reader can examine without asserting that the backlog cleared, the states matched, or the latches met a timing threshold.
Does the ‘40’ in BurstReplay-40 mean 40 bursts were tested?

Not from this artifact description. It explicitly gives a 40-µs replay budget and names the report BurstReplay-40, but it does not state a count of burst events or traces. Keep the number attached to the budget unless a separate record specifies a tested count.
What does a backlog record tell me in this report?

It shows outstanding replay work under the 40-µs budget at the points recorded. To interpret whether a candidate can cut over, a reader would need to relate that backlog to the sealed tick defining the proposed handoff. The artifact description says backlog was recorded; it does not state its values, whether it grew, or whether it drained.
Can I describe the report as showing that the replay budget is sufficient?

No. A report containing budget-backlog records is not, by itself, a finding that the budget cleared all required work before cutover. Sufficiency would require interpreting the recorded backlog together with the candidate-state comparisons and the relevant cutover boundaries. The artifact description provides the categories of information, not their outcomes.
Why include candidate-state comparisons alongside backlog?

They address a different condition. A clear backlog would suggest required logged work has been processed, while a candidate-state comparison asks whether that work produced the expected state at a particular boundary. Coalescing could process all recorded work yet still produce a state that does not match. The report contains both so those questions can be examined separately.
Does ‘candidate-state comparisons’ mean the candidate matched in every case?

No. ‘Comparisons’ names records of checking candidate state against a reference; it does not give the results of those checks. Do not turn a recorded comparison into an equality finding until the comparison outcomes are stated.
What is the role of physical latch intervals in this artifact?

They are timing observations of the actuator latch path while burst-write traces and the 40-µs replay budget are in use. They let a reader examine whether replay activity coincides with long gaps between physical latches. The artifact description does not provide a maximum interval, a 1 ms deadline-miss count, or an exactly-once latch conclusion.
Can the intervals by themselves show there were no missing or duplicate physical latches?

Not necessarily. An interval describes the time between observed latch events; deciding whether every required 1-ms tick had exactly one latch also needs association between events and ticks and confidence that the event record is complete. The report is described as containing physical latch intervals, not a completed per-tick latch-count audit.
Is the report about normal peak-load writes or burst-write traces?

The artifact description specifically says ‘under burst-write traces.’ The 40-µs budget comes from the activity being examined, but this report’s stated condition is burst writes. Avoid replacing that condition with a different workload label unless the report separately establishes it.
Does this report contain the raw state-write trace?

The description does not say it contains the raw trace. It says the backlog, candidate-state comparisons, and physical latch intervals were recorded *under* burst-write traces. You can identify the trace condition without claiming that every input write is itself reproduced in the report.
What if someone assumes the 40-µs budget is a measured replay cost?

Call it a ‘40-µs replay budget,’ not a 40-µs measured cost. A budget is the allowance used in the activity; actual per-tick work or backlog behavior would have to come from the records and their interpretation. The report description does not state a measured replay-cost value.
Does the artifact say anything about firmware-state pair selection after reset?

No. It describes backlog, candidate-state comparisons, and physical latch intervals under burst-write traces. It does not name reset injections, commit-record checks, or boot selection of a compatible firmware-state pair. Do not infer a recovery result from this report’s listed contents.
Give me a concise artifact-list entry without any implied pass result.

For the state-schema migration, I propose adding typed migration contracts for actuator-calibration bounds and pending-command ownership, checked against shadow state before atomic cutover. How should I describe that proposal?

Describe the contracts as conditions the migrated state must satisfy before it can become active. One contract checks that actuator-calibration values in the shadow state satisfy the bounds required by the candidate firmware. The other checks that pending-command ownership remains unambiguous across the handoff. Atomic cutover is permitted only after the shadow state passes both checks; a candidate that fails must not be partly selected.

This is a proposal for what to check, not a finding that any particular migration has passed. It does not specify the calibration bounds, the state types, or how pending commands are represented.
What does ‘typed’ add beyond a general statement that the migration is compatible?

It makes the expected structure and meaning of the relevant state explicit enough to check. The contract should identify which candidate-state values represent actuator calibration and which information establishes ownership of a pending command. That is more specific than saying the migrated bytes are readable.

Type agreement is not the whole check, though. A calibration value can have the expected type and still fall outside its permitted bounds. Ownership information can be well-formed and still assign a pending command ambiguously.
Are actuator-calibration bounds just a schema-format check?

No. A format check asks whether a value can be represented or decoded. A bounds check asks whether the value is acceptable under the candidate firmware’s actuator-calibration contract. The proposal needs both the relevant type and the applicable bound to be defined for the state actually being migrated. It supplies no numerical calibration limits, so none should be assumed.
Why check calibration before cutover instead of letting the candidate firmware discover a problem on its first tick?

Discovering incompatibility only after the candidate takes control would be too late for atomic rejection. The proposal checks the shadow state before the candidate becomes active, so a bounds failure prevents the firmware-state pair from being selected. It must not require the candidate to issue an actuator command before deciding whether its calibration state is acceptable.
Does ‘pending-command ownership’ mean validating the numerical value of the next actuator command?

No. It concerns who is authorized to handle a command that is pending at the handoff, and how that obligation relates to the cutover boundary. Checking a command’s numerical value would not by itself establish whether the old pair or the new pair owns it, whether it has already become effective, or whether it could be submitted twice. The ownership contract addresses that ambiguity.
Could a pending command simply be given to both firmware-state pairs so one is sure to handle it?

Not if that allows both to issue an effective command for the same obligation. The contract should establish one authorized owner for each pending command relevant to cutover. It also must not leave a required command with no owner. The purpose is to avoid both duplication and omission, not just to increase the chance that something is submitted.
What should the contract say about a command already issued by the current pair but not yet resolved at cutover?

It needs a defined treatment of that command’s ownership and status at the boundary. The candidate must not mistake it for a new command to issue again, and the current pair’s obligation must not simply disappear. The proposal does not specify where a command becomes effective or how its status is recorded, so those semantics have to be established before a concrete ownership check can be evaluated.
Isn't ownership already decided by swapping pairs at a tick boundary?

A tick-boundary swap identifies which pair should handle ticks on each side, but it does not automatically resolve a pending command associated with a tick near the boundary. The ownership contract checks whether the shadow state and proposed handoff agree on that unresolved obligation. Pair selection and command ownership need to describe the same boundary; otherwise a clean pair switch could still leave a command duplicated or unowned.
Could we check the shadow state once, long before the planned cutover, and rely on that verdict?

Only if the check remains valid for the state and pending-command situation at the actual cutover boundary. Live control may change state or command status after an earlier shadow-state check. The proposal calls for checking against shadow state *before atomic cutover*; that check needs to apply to the candidate state that would be selected and the pending ownership that would exist at that handoff. An earlier verdict alone should not be treated as proof about a changed boundary.
How does this fit with replaying state changes into shadow state?

The contracts should be assessed against the candidate state intended for cutover, including relevant changes incorporated before that boundary. Otherwise, the checks could validate a snapshot that no longer represents the state to be selected. Replaying deltas prepares the state; the typed contracts ask whether the prepared result satisfies the calibration and ownership conditions. Neither process gives the candidate actuator authority before cutover.
If coalescing changes the way writes are replayed, can we check the contracts on the uncoalesced snapshot instead?

That would not establish that the *resulting* shadow state satisfies them. The candidate selected at cutover is what matters. Whatever preparation produces that candidate state, its actuator-calibration values and pending-command ownership must meet the contracts before atomic selection. This proposal does not prescribe a coalescing algorithm or claim that one preserves these properties automatically.
What exactly would failure of the calibration-bounds contract require?

The incompatible shadow migration must not proceed to atomic cutover. In particular, an out-of-bounds candidate calibration must not be installed while leaving the candidate firmware inactive, or vice versa. The active firmware-state pair remains the selected pair as the candidate is rejected. That is the proposed pre-cutover rejection behavior; no particular out-of-bounds value has been supplied.
And what would failure of the pending-command ownership contract require?

The candidate likewise must not be selected at that proposed boundary. If ownership cannot be assigned unambiguously without a duplicate or missing command, the cutover condition has not been satisfied. Rejecting or deferring that cutover must not itself abandon a command the current pair is responsible for. The proposal does not specify whether a particular ownership failure can later be resolved, so it should not promise a remedy.
Are the two contracts independent?

They test distinct conditions: acceptable calibration values and unambiguous ownership of pending commands. Both have to hold for the proposed cutover. Passing the calibration check cannot excuse an ownership failure, and a well-defined command owner cannot make an out-of-bounds calibration acceptable. Their interaction may matter in a concrete state schema, but none is specified here.
Does a typed contract guarantee that the migration code itself is correct?

No. It supplies conditions to check on the shadow state and proposed ownership at cutover. Passing those conditions would not, by itself, establish that every possible state value was migrated correctly or that every control deadline is met. The contract must accurately capture the requirements it is meant to enforce, and its checks must apply to the state that will actually be selected.
Could the shadow state satisfy its types but lose an important pending command entirely?

That is why the ownership contract cannot be reduced to checking that a field has the expected type. It must address the pending obligations relevant to the boundary: a command that needs to be handled cannot vanish merely because the candidate representation is well-formed. Conversely, one obligation must not appear as two effective commands. The proposal does not provide a command inventory or its encoding, so the exact check remains to be defined.
Should pending-command ownership be checked against both the old and candidate pairs?

The check has to make sense across their handoff. Shadow state describes what the candidate would inherit, but a pending command may belong to work assigned to the current pair. A valid ownership determination must account for that existing obligation and specify whether the candidate has any corresponding obligation after cutover, without double assignment or an unowned gap. Checking candidate fields in isolation would not settle that relationship.
If the current pair has already completed its last command, can the candidate own the next one?

That is the intended kind of boundary, provided completion and the next obligation are defined consistently with the actuator path. The contract would need to establish that the current pair’s command is not still pending in a way the candidate could replay, and that the next required command has an authorized owner. This is a conditional illustration, not a report that a particular handoff has reached that state.
Does the proposal require stopping the 1-ms scheduler to run these checks?

No. The uninterrupted-update requirement still applies while shadow-state validation runs: each 1 ms control deadline must be met without skipped or duplicated actuator commands. The checks need to be scheduled and coordinated with the control path accordingly. Calling them pre-cutover checks does not establish their execution cost or authorize a pause.
Would atomic cutover itself establish that the calibration and ownership contracts were checked?

No. Atomicity says the selected pair changes as a unit; it does not say the candidate was suitable to select. The proposal requires the typed contracts to be checked against shadow state *before* that atomic change. A perfectly atomic selection of out-of-bounds calibration or ambiguous command ownership would still violate the intended condition.
How should this affect an update-time reset while the contract check is unfinished?

An unfinished check must not be mistaken for validation of a candidate firmware-state pair. After an update-time reset, boot still needs a compatible committed pair; a partially checked shadow state is not one merely because it is present. These contracts add pre-cutover conditions, while recoverable pair selection remains a separate requirement. The proposal does not specify new reset-persistence machinery.
Can these checks prove that after reset the last committed pair will boot?

No. They concern actuator-calibration bounds and pending-command ownership in shadow state before cutover. Whether boot identifies a committed compatible firmware-state pair after a reset depends on the commitment and recovery rule. Do not use a successful pre-cutover contract check as a substitute for observing or establishing boot selection.
How would I frame a test without inventing particular calibration values or command states?

Define test cases from the actual schema and command-ownership semantics when they are available. Check that a shadow state meeting both contracts can be considered for cutover, while a state violating the applicable calibration bounds or leaving pending-command ownership ambiguous cannot be selected. At each attempted cutover, also observe that rejection does not partly change the active pair or disrupt required 1-ms ticks. Those are checks to design, not experiments or outcomes supplied by this proposal.
If a candidate passes both checks, may I say it is ready for atomic cutover?

You may say it passes *these two pre-cutover conditions*. Readiness also requires that the candidate state is coherent at the chosen boundary, that its firmware-state migration is otherwise compatible, and that the handoff can preserve the 1 ms deadline and actuator consistency. Passing the typed contracts should not be expanded into an unconditional claim that every cutover condition has been met.
Give me a compact proposal statement that preserves both contract subjects and their timing.

Add typed migration contracts for actuator-calibration bounds and pending-command ownership, and check them against the shadow state that would be selected before atomic firmware-state-pair cutover. Reject a candidate that fails either check without partially changing the active pair; the contracts and their outcomes remain to be specified and verified.

My hypothesis is that typed migration contracts will reject invalid actuator calibration and ambiguous pending-command ownership before commit without missing 1-ms latch deadlines. How should I formulate it?

Keep the two rejection conditions and the timing condition explicit: ‘We hypothesize that typed migration contracts checked before commit will reject candidate states with invalid actuator calibration or ambiguous pending-command ownership, while actuator latches continue meeting their 1-ms deadlines.’ This is a proposed outcome to test, not an established rejection or timing result.
Is ‘invalid calibration’ the same as a state value of the wrong type?

Not necessarily. A calibration value could have the expected type but violate the bounds required by the candidate firmware. Conversely, a value that cannot be interpreted under the contract could also be invalid. The hypothesis does not specify calibration fields, bounds, or particular invalid values, so leave those to the contract definition rather than inventing examples as though they were requirements.
What makes pending-command ownership ambiguous?

Ambiguity means the contract cannot establish one authorized owner for a pending actuator-command obligation at the handoff. It must rule out both a situation in which two firmware-state pairs could effectively handle the same obligation and one in which neither would handle it. The hypothesis does not specify a pending-command representation, so the concrete ambiguity tests remain to be defined.
Why say ‘before commit’ rather than ‘before the next actuator command’?

Because the stated hypothesis requires incompatible candidate state to be rejected before the firmware-state pair is committed. ‘Before the next actuator command’ would express a different ordering and might still allow an invalid pair to become committed. The contract checks need to prevent invalid calibration or ambiguous ownership from entering the committed pair in the first place.
Would it be acceptable for a contract to detect a problem after commit but before cutover?

That would not meet the ‘reject before commit’ condition as stated. Even if control had not yet changed pairs, committing an invalid candidate would change what recovery might regard as eligible. The hypothesis proposes screening those conditions before commitment, so a later detection cannot be described as confirmation of it.
Does rejection require deleting all shadow migration work?

The hypothesis requires the invalid candidate not to reach commitment; it does not specify how temporary shadow data is handled. The externally important point is that rejected candidate state cannot become the active or committed firmware-state pair. Cleanup details would depend on the implementation and should not be added as if the hypothesis had decided them.
If calibration fails but ownership passes, should the candidate be committed?

No. The hypothesis says the contracts reject invalid calibration *and* ambiguous ownership before commit. Each is an independent reason not to commit the candidate pair. Passing one check does not override failure of the other.
And if ownership is ambiguous but calibration is within bounds?

The candidate should likewise be rejected before commit under the hypothesis. In-bounds calibration does not supply a unique owner for a pending command. If the ownership obligation is unresolved, commitment cannot be treated as safe merely because the other contract passes.
What is the latch-deadline part actually claiming?

It claims that performing the typed checks and handling rejection will not make any applicable actuator latch miss its 1-ms deadline during uninterrupted control. That is separate from detecting incompatibility. A contract could correctly reject an invalid candidate yet consume enough time or create enough interference for a latch to run late; the hypothesis predicts that both rejection and timely latching can hold together.
Does ‘without missing 1-ms latch deadlines’ also prove that no actuator command is duplicated?

No. Timeliness and exactly-once behavior are different properties. A latch could occur before its deadline yet be duplicated, and a single latch could occur late. The hypothesis explicitly names the 1-ms latch deadline condition and rejection of ambiguous ownership, but a no-duplicate command finding would require observing or establishing the actual command and latch ownership behavior.
Could the contract checks be performed on an early shadow snapshot and count as precommit validation?

Only if that snapshot still represents the state whose pair would be committed, including the relevant calibration and pending-command ownership at the commit boundary. Control can continue changing state or completing commands while checks run. A precommit verdict about an outdated snapshot would not establish that the candidate actually committed satisfies the contracts.
So should the hypothesis mention checking the final shadow state rather than just an initial one?

That would make its meaning clearer. The typed contracts should be checked against the candidate state intended for commitment, with ownership interpreted at the relevant handoff boundary. The statement need not prescribe how that state is brought current; it just should not imply that an old snapshot verdict automatically remains valid after additional control ticks.
Does a typed contract need to encode physical actuator behavior?

It needs to express the calibration and ownership conditions it is meant to check. A contract verdict on state is not the same thing as a physical latch observation. The timing part of the hypothesis therefore needs separate evidence about 1-ms latch deadlines; type and bounds checks alone cannot establish physical timing.
How might we test the hypothesis while keeping those observations separate?

Exercise candidate states that violate the defined calibration contract and candidate states whose pending-command ownership violates its defined uniqueness condition. For each, check whether rejection occurs before commit and whether the active compatible pair remains in control. Independently observe actuator latch timing against each applicable 1-ms deadline while the check and rejection occur. This describes the kinds of observations needed; it does not assume test cases, counts, or outcomes that have not been supplied.
Would a validator returning ‘reject’ be enough evidence?

It would address the validator’s verdict, but not by itself prove the candidate was never committed, nor that actuator latches met their 1-ms deadlines. The hypothesis has an ordering claim and a physical timing claim in addition to a classification claim. Evidence for each should be recorded at the relevant point rather than inferred from the return value.
What if the active pair remains the same but a commit record briefly names the rejected candidate?

Then the before-commit rejection condition would need careful scrutiny. An unchanged active pair does not prove that an invalid candidate was never made recoverably committed. Under this hypothesis, invalid calibration or ambiguous ownership must be rejected before commit, not merely kept inactive until later. That is a conditional interpretation of a possible outcome, not a report that it happened.
Is the hypothesis about reset recovery too?

It is about precommit rejection and uninterrupted 1-ms latch deadlines. Rejecting an invalid pair before commit is relevant to what might be eligible for recovery, but the statement does not test or guarantee which compatible pair boots after an update-time reset. Boot selection remains a distinct recovery question.
Can I say the contracts will catch every possible schema incompatibility?

No. The hypothesis specifically names invalid actuator calibration and ambiguous pending-command ownership. It does not assert that those contracts cover all possible state-schema incompatibilities. Preserve those two subjects rather than broadening the claim to complete migration correctness.
Would stating ‘zero missed deadlines’ be appropriate at this point?

Only as a predicted outcome within the hypothesis, not as an observed result: ‘we hypothesize there will be no missed 1-ms latch deadlines while these invalid migrations are rejected.’ Without a reported test, writing ‘zero missed deadlines’ as a finding would overstate the evidence.
Give me a final hypothesis sentence that includes the contract subjects, the precommit condition, and the timing claim.

We hypothesize that typed migration contracts applied to the candidate shadow state will reject invalid actuator calibration and ambiguous pending-command ownership before commit, without causing actuator latches to miss their 1-ms deadlines.

Let's run ContractFault-200 with out-of-range actuator calibration and duplicate command owners. Under peak load, we'll inspect the commit records and physical latch intervals. How should I describe the activity?

Describe it as a fault-injection and inspection activity: ‘Run ContractFault-200 under peak load with out-of-range actuator-calibration state and duplicate command ownership. Inspect the commit records to assess whether those candidates were committed, and inspect physical actuator latch intervals to assess timing during the checks.’ The run is intended to evaluate precommit rejection without missed 1-ms latch deadlines; no verdict or timing outcome is supplied yet.
What does ‘out-of-range’ mean if we haven't specified calibration limits here?

It means outside the applicable actuator-calibration bounds defined by the contract for the candidate state. The activity does not supply numerical bounds or particular injected values. The run needs to identify the actual bounds it applies so that an out-of-range case is interpretable, but the description should not invent them.
And do duplicate command owners mean two actuator commands were actually issued?

No. Duplicate owners describe an invalid ownership assignment: more than one owner is designated for the same pending-command obligation. That is the fault being exercised. It does not, by itself, report two issued commands, two physical latches, or a repeated actuator output. Those would be separate observed outcomes.
Why inspect commit records instead of relying on a contract's rejection verdict?

The precommit claim concerns what happened to the candidate pair, not only what a checker reported. A rejection verdict alone would not show whether a commit record nonetheless made that candidate eligible for selection. Examining the records helps assess whether an invalid calibration or duplicate-owner candidate was kept out of the committed firmware-state pairs. The activity does not yet report what those records show.
If a commit record still names the existing compatible pair, does that prove the candidate was rejected before commit?

It is relevant, but interpret it in the context of record coverage and ordering. A record showing the existing pair at one observation point does not necessarily exclude an intervening commitment or prove when a contract verdict occurred. The check should establish whether the faulted candidate ever became committed and how the relevant record states relate to the attempted commitment. Do not infer a complete ordering solely from a final record value.
What if the invalid candidate's data is present somewhere, but no commit record selects it?

Presence of candidate data is different from a completed commitment. The precommit-rejection question is whether the out-of-range or duplicate-owner candidate became a committed firmware-state pair. An unselected shadow candidate should not be described as committed simply because some of its data is present. Conversely, an apparently unselected candidate does not establish a successful contract check unless the relevant verdict and commitment ordering can be determined.
Could we treat a CRC-valid commit record as proof that the calibration contract passed?

No. CRC validity and the typed migration contract answer different questions. A CRC check concerns record integrity under its definition; the calibration contract concerns whether the candidate state satisfies its bounds. The run should not infer an in-range calibration value, or a unique pending-command owner, from record readability alone.
Why measure physical latch intervals during a migration-contract test?

The contracts may be checked while control continues under peak load. Physical latch intervals give timing observations along the actuator path during that work. The question is whether checking and handling the faulted candidates can coexist with the 1-ms latch deadlines. Rejecting invalid state correctly would not excuse an actuator latch that misses its deadline.
If every physical latch interval is below 1 ms, can I report zero missed latch deadlines?

Only if the measurement definition and tick association justify that conclusion. An interval measures spacing between observed physical latch events; a deadline concerns when the latch required for a particular 1-ms tick occurred. Keep the observed interval results distinct from a deadline-miss count unless the run establishes that relationship. The activity does not give either result in advance.
Would latch intervals tell us whether any tick latched twice?

Not automatically. Intervals describe the timing of observed events. To identify a duplicate latch, the physical events must also be assigned to their required ticks and counted. In particular, the injected duplicate-owner condition does not mean an extra latch occurred; inspecting timing should not silently be reported as an exactly-once latch audit without the needed event-to-tick information.
Does peak load apply to both fault types?

The stated activity runs ContractFault-200 under peak load with out-of-range calibration and duplicate command owners. When recording outcomes, keep the load condition associated with the fault cases actually exercised. A candidate pair can satisfy a state-compatibility check while the handoff still lacks a clear command for its next assigned tick. Both conditions must hold before cutover is enabled.
Does ‘ready commands’ imply that core 1 has already sent future commands to the actuator?

No. Readiness is not physical dispatch. It means the required command obligations can be served under the tick ownership rule if cutover occurs. Core 0 remains the proposed dispatch point. Issuing future commands prematurely could duplicate a tick's effective command or blur which firmware-state pair owns it; the proposal does not authorize that.
Could we define readiness as ‘there is some command value available’?

That would be too weak. Readiness needs to be associated with the tick that would be assigned after cutover and with the validated firmware-state pair that would control it. An available value with no clear tick association does not establish that the next required command will be dispatched once and on time. The proposal does not specify how command readiness is represented, so its precise test remains to be defined.
How would the two cores agree on when the candidate may take over?

They need one cutover decision that applies to a defined tick boundary: the candidate pair has passed validation, the relevant commands are ready, and core 0 can assign the adjacent ticks without duplicate or missing actuator dispatch. Core 1 can prepare and communicate readiness, but that communication must not itself change the command owner midway through a tick. The specific coordination method is not selected by the proposal.
If core 1 announces that the pair is validated during a tick, should we switch right then?

Not solely on that announcement. The proposal requires command readiness as well as pair validation, and the transfer of ownership must preserve the tick-indexed command sequence. A verdict arriving during a tick can make the candidate eligible for consideration at an appropriate boundary; it does not make an immediate mid-tick change safe.
What if the command for the first candidate-owned tick is not ready at the planned boundary?

Then the proposed cutover gate has not been satisfied at that boundary. The existing compatible pair must retain responsibility for ticks it continues to own; assigning the next tick to an unready candidate would risk skipping its command. The proposal does not require cutover at a fixed time, and waiting for a suitable boundary must not be confused with pausing 1 ms control.
Can core 0 just repeat the preceding command value while it waits for a candidate command?

The proposal does not equate repeating an old command with serving the next tick's required command. Identical actuator values across ticks could be legitimate if each tick has its own authorized command, but replaying a command assigned to an earlier tick does not establish command readiness for a later tick. If the candidate is unready, cutover should not be enabled merely because core 0 could resend or hold an old value.
How does the tick index help at the exact handoff?

Imagine an illustrative boundary between ticks N and N+1. The old pair owns the command obligation for N; if cutover is enabled at that boundary, the validated candidate pair owns the obligation for N+1. Core 0 dispatches according to that ownership, without accepting another effective command for N or proceeding past N+1 without its command. The tick labels are only a way to express the rule; the proposal does not prescribe a counter layout or a command protocol.
Could core 0 dispatch a command for N+1 that core 1 prepared before the switch?

Only if the prepared command is the authorized one for N+1 under the candidate pair that actually becomes selected, and the readiness and cutover rules establish that relationship. Preparation on core 1 does not by itself grant dispatch authority. Core 0 remains the dispatching core, and the candidate state and command used after the boundary must correspond to the same validated handoff.
What if the shadow state changes after the pair passes validation but before the first candidate command is ready?

The cutover condition must apply to the pair and command situation that will actually exist at the boundary. A validation verdict for an earlier state cannot automatically cover changed candidate state, and a command prepared from the earlier state cannot automatically be assumed suitable for a later one. If the necessary correspondence cannot be established, do not enable cutover on the old verdict or an unmatched ready-command indication.
Would two cores by themselves keep the 1 ms deadline?

No. Work on core 1 may still contend with core 0 for resources, and the cutover decision may impose work on the dispatch path. The design has to account for the effects of migration, validation, readiness signaling, and the handoff on every uninterrupted 1 ms control interval. Assigning migration to a separate core is a proposed way to reduce interference, not a measured deadline guarantee.
Does core 0 need to stop dispatching while core 1 validates the candidate?

No. The intended split is that core 0 keeps dispatching the ticks belonging to the active pair while core 1 prepares the candidate. A validation check must not force a missed deadline or a skipped actuator command. The candidate only enters the dispatch sequence when both cutover conditions are satisfied and ownership changes at a coherent boundary.
If the migration is incompatible, what happens to the tick-indexed command sequence?

It continues under the currently selected compatible pair. An incompatible candidate does not satisfy the validated-pair condition, so it cannot trigger cutover. Rejection must not partially select the candidate or transfer command ownership; core 0 still has to dispatch one authorized command for each applicable tick within its 1 ms deadline.
Do we need to distinguish a command being ready from one being physically dispatched?

Yes. Readiness is a precondition for assigning a future tick to the candidate. Dispatch is core 0's action for that assigned tick, and effective actuator behavior is a further observation along the command path. A ready command might never be dispatched if cutover does not occur; conversely, saying a command was ready does not prove it reached the actuator exactly once or met its deadline.
Would contiguous tick indices alone demonstrate actuator consistency?

No. Indices can be contiguous even if a command is not effectively dispatched for one of them, or if a command is duplicated under the same index. To assess the proposal, relate each required tick to its authorized pair and to the effective actuator command core 0 dispatches, checking for both gaps and duplicates. The index is a means of relating those events, not a replacement for observing them.
Where do pending commands fit if a cutover is requested near a dispatch?

A pending command must retain its assigned tick and ownership through the decision. The handoff cannot let a command from the old pair become an extra command after selection changes, and it cannot discard the only command owed for the boundary tick. The ready-command gate has to account for any such pending obligation. The proposal does not specify the command-status representation or when physical dispatch is considered complete.
Does the proposal say which core commits the firmware-state pair?

No. It allocates actuator-command dispatch to core 0 and firmware migration to core 1, and conditions cutover on validated pairs and ready commands. It does not assign a particular core to persist the pair commitment or define its storage sequence. Any implementation of commitment must still keep the selected firmware and state compatible, including after an update-time reset.
Would meeting the ready-command condition prove reset recovery?

No. Command readiness concerns a proposed uninterrupted cutover. After a reset, boot must still identify a compatible committed firmware-state pair. Having prepared commands before the reset does not itself establish what pair was recoverably committed, nor does a compatible boot by itself establish an uninterrupted sequence of actuator commands through the reset.
What should a test of this two-core proposal measure?

Under uninterrupted update activity, check each applicable 1 ms deadline and associate each tick with exactly one effective actuator command dispatched through core 0. At proposed cutovers, check that the selected firmware-state pair has a completed validation result, the first candidate-owned tick has a ready authorized command, and no old-pair command is replayed or required command skipped. Separately, reset-recovery tests would check that boot selects a compatible committed pair. These are verification questions for the proposal, not outcomes it has already achieved.
Can you summarize the cutover gate in one rule?

Enable cutover only at a tick boundary where the candidate firmware-state pair is validated for the state being selected and the commands needed for the new ownership interval are ready; core 0 then continues the tick-indexed actuator sequence with one effective command per required 1 ms tick. Core 1's migration work must not interrupt that dispatch path, and the timing and exactly-once properties still need to be demonstrated.
How can core 0 consume core 1’s prepared command without stale-cache reads or delaying the 1-ms latch?

The handoff needs two separate guarantees: core 0 must see the fully prepared command for the intended tick, and checking or consuming it must have a bounded cost that preserves the 1-ms latch deadline. Core 1 should not signal command readiness until the command contents are complete and visible to core 0 under the controller’s memory-sharing rules. Core 0 should use the command only if that readiness indication still corresponds to the tick and validated firmware-state pair it is about to dispatch.

Those are requirements on a possible cross-core handoff, not evidence that a particular cache arrangement or signaling method already satisfies them.
Why isn't it enough for core 1 to write the command and then set a ready flag?

The order in which core 1 performs writes does not necessarily establish the order in which core 0 can observe them. Core 0 might see a readiness indication while still seeing older command contents unless publication and consumption have appropriate visibility and ordering semantics. The ready indication must mean that the complete command it names is available to core 0, not merely that core 1 has finished executing its own writes.
What would the ready indication need to identify?

At minimum, it must be interpretable for the specific command obligation core 0 is about to serve: the assigned tick and the firmware-state pair whose command is authorized. It also has to refer to the completed command contents, rather than an earlier or partly overwritten preparation. The question does not specify a flag format or a particular memory layout; these are relationships the implementation must make unambiguous.
If core 0 sees ‘ready,’ can it immediately assume the command is current?

Not without checking what that indication covers. A ready command for an earlier tick is stale for the current tick even if its contents are visible. A ready command prepared for a different candidate state may likewise not be the one authorized at cutover. Visibility, freshness, and ownership are distinct: core 0 needs the complete contents, the correct tick association, and a pair that is validated and selected for that tick.
Could a cache-coherence mechanism alone settle all three?

No. Cache coherence can be part of establishing what data one core sees after another publishes it, but it does not by itself decide which tick a command belongs to or whether the candidate pair has cutover authority. The publication rule and the tick-ownership rule must agree. The controller’s actual memory model and cache behavior would determine what operations are necessary to provide the visibility guarantee; none is specified here.
What if core 0 reads the command fields, and core 1 modifies them during that read?

Then core 0 could consume a mixture of command contents, even if each individual read succeeds. The prepared command needs a stable view while core 0 consumes it, or the consumption rule needs to detect that the view changed and refuse it. Core 1’s later preparation must not silently alter the command that an existing readiness indication authorizes. How to provide a stable view is an implementation choice.
Could core 0 simply keep rereading until the command stops changing?

An unbounded retry loop would be problematic for a 1-ms latch deadline. Even if repeated reads eventually obtain a stable command, ‘eventually’ does not establish that the correct command was available in time for its tick. The control path needs a bounded readiness and consumption procedure, and a prospective cutover should not assign the candidate a tick it cannot serve on time.
Would waiting briefly for core 1’s command be acceptable at the boundary?

Only if the wait and all other control-path work are bounded so that the required latch still meets its 1-ms deadline. The proposal’s cutover gate is meant to avoid depending on a command becoming ready after core 0 needs it. If readiness cannot be established in time, a cutover to the candidate at that boundary cannot be justified by hoping the wait is short.
If the candidate's command isn't ready, can core 0 just skip the tick and pick up at the next one?

No. Skipping a required actuator command conflicts with the uninterrupted-update requirement. The gate should leave the current compatible pair in charge of a tick if the candidate is not ready to own it. That still requires the current pair to serve its tick on time; declining a cutover is not permission to pause control.
Could core 0 use the previous tick’s command instead while the new command becomes visible?

A command assigned to an earlier tick is not automatically the authorized command for this one. Two successive commands might legitimately carry the same value, but that is different from replaying an old command or treating a cached value as evidence that the next command was produced. Core 0 must know which command belongs to the current tick; stale-cache avoidance is therefore about command identity and contents, not only about whether the numerical value looks plausible.
What does ‘consume’ mean here: reading the bytes, accepting the command, or physically latching it?

Those should be distinguished. Core 0 first observes a prepared command and its readiness, then decides whether it is authorized for the tick, then dispatches it through the actuator path. The physical latch is a further event with its own deadline. A successful read does not prove timely dispatch or a timely physical latch, and a command described as ‘ready’ has not thereby been latched.
Could core 0 read the ready indication and the command in whichever order is convenient?

The order has to follow whatever publication-and-consumption rule establishes a consistent view. In general, the readiness check must not be treated as proof of complete contents if subsequent reads may still see an older or partially prepared command. A proposed implementation must specify the memory-ordering and visibility guarantees it relies on, then verify that core 0's reads use them correctly. The question does not select a particular ordering primitive.
Would adding a cache flush on core 1 automatically solve the problem?

Not automatically. Its effect would depend on the controller’s memory and cache rules, and it would still need to be paired with a readiness rule that core 0 interprets correctly. Moreover, any visibility operation that stalls core 0 or delays the latch must be accounted for against the 1-ms deadline. Naming an operation does not establish that command contents are current, stable, tick-matched, and available in time.
What if the command is visible, but the validation verdict belongs to an older shadow generation?

Then visibility does not make the command eligible for cutover. The pair and state used to prepare the command need to correspond to a candidate that is validated for the state actually selected. A command can be fully present in shared memory while its associated candidate has not satisfied the cutover condition. Core 0 should not turn a visible command into actuator authority without that match.
How do we avoid a race where core 0 verifies a ready command and core 1 replaces it immediately afterward?

The verification must identify a stable command view that remains the one core 0 consumes. If core 1 prepares a later command, it must not overwrite the still-authorized view in a way that changes what core 0 dispatches after its check. Otherwise the check-to-consumption interval could produce the same kind of mismatch as a stale-cache read. The exact synchronization method depends on the implementation, but a race-free correspondence between checked readiness and consumed contents is required.
Does handing the candidate the next tick mean core 1 can issue that tick’s actuator command as well?

No. In the proposed split, core 1 prepares a command and core 0 dispatches tick-indexed actuator commands. Preparation must not create a second physical issuer. For the first candidate-owned tick, core 0 should dispatch one authorized prepared command; it must not accept a late old-pair submission as an additional command, and core 1 must not independently dispatch the prepared one.
Can a command be ready for tick N+1 before tick N has physically latched?

Preparation and authority are different. A candidate command for a prospective N+1 can be prepared in advance, but that does not authorize dispatch for N+1 before the handoff conditions are met or remove the old pair’s obligation for N. The handoff must relate the readiness indication, tick ownership, and completion of the relevant latch obligation so neither tick is replayed or omitted. N and N+1 are only illustrative labels.
If core 0's readiness check is quick, does that prove the physical latch will meet the deadline?

No. The check is only part of the path to the physical latch. Even a bounded, correct cross-core read could be followed by dispatch or latch work that misses the 1-ms deadline. The timing argument must include the relevant visibility and synchronization costs as well as the rest of the latch path. Conversely, a timely latch observation does not by itself prove that core 0 never read stale command data.
What would we need to observe to test both the stale-read and timing concerns?

For each proposed boundary, relate the command core 1 finished preparing to the command core 0 actually consumed and dispatched, including its tick and validated-pair association. Check that core 0 never treats an incomplete, old, or mismatched command as ready. Separately associate physical latch events with their ticks and examine their timing against the 1-ms deadline, including the first tick after cutover. These are tests to perform, not outcomes already established for the two-core proposal.
Does a contiguous series of tick indices prove core 0 never read stale data?

No. Indices could be contiguous while command contents came from an older preparation, or while one tick’s physical output was repeated. A useful trace must distinguish the identity and contents of the command authorized for a tick from what core 0 actually consumed, as well as what reached the actuator. Sequence numbering alone cannot settle data visibility or physical latch timing.
Should core 0 perform the full migration-contract validation itself before accepting the command?

That would put potentially substantial validation work on the time-critical dispatch path. The proposal places migration on core 1 and enables cutover only for validated pairs and ready commands. Core 0 needs a bounded way to establish that those conditions apply to the particular command and state it is selecting; it should not assume that repeating the full validation within a 1-ms tick is free. The form and measured cost of that bounded check remain to be established.
What about a reset during the publication of a prepared command?

The stale-cache and latch question concerns an uninterrupted cross-core handoff. A reset introduces a separate recovery obligation: boot must identify a compatible committed firmware-state pair, not treat a partly prepared command as proof that the candidate was committed. The question does not specify command continuity through the reset itself, and a correct ready-command publication rule would not by itself establish compatible boot recovery.
Can you put the proposed cross-core rule in one concise statement?

Core 1 may publish a complete, stable command for an identified tick and validated firmware-state pair; core 0 may consume and dispatch it only after a visibility-safe, bounded readiness check confirms that same command is authorized for its tick. If that condition is not met at the boundary, do not transfer tick ownership to the candidate. The whole path to the physical latch must still meet the 1-ms deadline, with neither a duplicate nor a skipped actuator command.

To handle the cross-core handoff, I plan to implement uncached, tick-tagged mailboxes with release/acquire publication. We'll retain the old firmware until the prepared command is ready, then benchmark core-0 latch latency. How should I describe the plan?

State the mechanism, the cutover condition, and the measurement separately: ‘Implement uncached, tick-tagged mailboxes for prepared commands, using release/acquire publication between the preparing and consuming cores. Keep the old firmware responsible for control until the command needed for cutover is ready. Then benchmark core-0 latch latency, including the handoff.’ This is a plan to address stale reads and timing; it is not yet evidence that the mailbox is safe or that the 1 ms latch deadline is met.
Why specify an uncached mailbox if we're also specifying release/acquire publication?

They address related but different concerns. The uncached mailbox is the proposed shared-memory location from which core 0 reads the prepared command. Release/acquire publication is the proposed ordering rule: core 1 completes the command contents before publishing readiness, and core 0 observes that publication before consuming the contents.

Neither label alone proves the intended visibility on the actual controller. The memory attributes, publication operations, and compiler and hardware behavior must support the ordering being relied upon.
What should the tick tag tell core 0?

It should identify the control tick for which the prepared command is intended. Core 0 must not accept a visible command merely because a mailbox says it is ready; the tag must match the tick core 0 is assigning to that command. A command prepared for an earlier tick is not the next tick’s command simply because it is still in shared memory.
Can the tick tag alone indicate that the candidate firmware-state pair is validated?

No. A tick tag identifies the command’s intended tick. Cutover also requires a validated firmware-state pair and a ready command corresponding to that pair. The plan names a tick-tagged mailbox, not a complete encoding of pair validation in the tag. Whatever readiness core 0 relies on must be associated with the pair actually selected as well as the tick it will serve.
What exactly is published with release semantics?

The intended sequence is that core 1 finishes preparing the command information for a tick and then publishes an indication that this completed information is ready. Release semantics apply to that publication so the preceding preparation is ordered before it. Core 0 uses acquire semantics when observing readiness before reading the associated command.

The plan does not specify the mailbox layout or the exact publication variable. A concrete implementation must define which data a readiness indication covers and prevent it from authorizing a partly written command.
If core 0 performs an acquire read, does that mean the command cannot change afterward?

No. Acquire addresses ordering and visibility of writes that were published before the corresponding release; it does not by itself make mailbox contents immutable. The plan also needs a rule that keeps the published command stable while core 0 consumes it, or reliably detects a changed view before dispatch. Otherwise core 0 could see a valid readiness indication and still consume data that core 1 subsequently replaced.
Would using an uncached region prevent that replacement problem?

No. Uncached access can address a stale-cache concern, but it does not settle concurrent ownership of the mailbox. Core 1 must not overwrite an already published command in a way that changes what core 0 is about to dispatch. Publication and stable consumption are separate parts of a correct handoff.
What does ‘retain old firmware until ready’ mean for command ownership?

Until the cutover condition is satisfied at an appropriate tick boundary, the currently selected firmware-state pair remains responsible for its assigned ticks and core 0 continues dispatching their commands. The candidate’s prepared command does not gain actuator authority merely by existing in a mailbox. If the command required for the prospective first candidate-owned tick is not ready, that tick must not be transferred to an unready candidate.
Does retaining the old firmware mean we have to stop preparing the candidate?

No. Core 1 can continue migration and command preparation while the current pair remains responsible for control. ‘Retain until ready’ concerns which pair may be selected for upcoming ticks; it does not forbid off-path preparation. That preparation must still avoid interfering with the active 1 ms control deadlines.
Can core 0 wait at the tick boundary for the ready flag to appear?

An unbounded wait would risk delaying the 1 ms latch. The proposed rule should make readiness a condition for transferring ownership, rather than an expectation that core 0 will block until core 1 finishes. If the candidate is not ready at a suitable boundary, the old pair remains responsible for control. The benchmark should account for any readiness check or bounded coordination that does occur on core 0.
If the mailbox is ready one tick early, can core 0 dispatch that command early?

No. Readiness means the command can be considered when its tagged tick becomes assigned to the candidate; it does not advance the actuator-command sequence. Core 0 must dispatch according to tick ownership and the relevant latch timing. A command tagged for a future tick should not become an additional command for the current one.
What if a ready mailbox contains the right tick tag but a command derived from an earlier shadow state?

A matching tick tag alone would not establish that the command belongs to the validated firmware-state pair being selected. The readiness and cutover decision must refer to the state that actually supplies the command. If the pair or candidate state has changed since preparation and that correspondence cannot be established, the prepared command should not authorize cutover for that tick. The plan does not prescribe how that association is represented.
Is it enough to benchmark the mailbox read time?

No. The planned measurement is **core-0 latch latency**, not just the time to read mailbox data. The relevant path includes whatever core 0 must do to observe publication, confirm that readiness and the tick tag apply, dispatch the authorized command, and reach the latch event being timed. Measuring only a fast acquire read would not establish that the physical latch meets its 1 ms obligation.
Where should the benchmark start and stop?

Define endpoints that make the reported number a meaningful core-0 latch latency for its assigned tick. The start should be tied to the tick’s control or dispatch obligation, and the end to the latch event the deadline concerns. If the measurement stops when core 0 merely reads a command or submits it, call it that narrower latency rather than physical latch latency. The plan leaves instrumentation and endpoints to be specified.
Should the benchmark focus only on a successful cutover?

The boundary where the candidate is ready matters, but so does a boundary where it is not ready and the old pair continues. Both paths can impose a readiness check on core 0. Measuring the running control path around the decision helps assess whether retaining the old firmware actually avoids a late latch; the plan itself gives no outcome for either path.
Would an average below 1 ms be enough for the timing claim?

No. Averages can conceal an individual latch at or beyond its 1 ms deadline. Examine the latency of the affected ticks, including those adjacent to the handoff, and make clear whether the measurements cover the entire interval relevant to the deadline. The benchmark is intended to obtain those observations; it does not supply a measured maximum yet.
If every measured latch is timely, would that also rule out stale-cache reads?

No. Timing and data correctness require separate checks. Core 0 could latch on time while consuming the wrong tick’s command or older command contents. The uncached mailbox and release/acquire rule are meant to address visibility; the benchmark measures latch timing. The published and consumed command identities and contents would need to agree to assess the stale-read concern.
What if the mailbox read is current, but core 0 issues the same tick’s command twice?

Then the visibility mechanism did not establish the separate exactly-once requirement. A tick tag can help core 0 recognize which obligation a command serves, but the dispatch path must still avoid duplicate effective commands and ensure no required tick is skipped. The latch-latency benchmark by itself would not establish the count of commands per tick.
Does ‘old firmware until ready’ guarantee the actuator sequence has no gaps?

Not by itself. It avoids transferring a tick to a candidate without a ready command, but the old pair must actually continue supplying each tick it owns, and the handoff must assign the next tick unambiguously. The plan proposes a readiness gate; exactly-once actuator behavior still has to be checked at the boundary.
Could a ready indication from an earlier tick linger and accidentally authorize cutover?

That is why tick tagging matters. Core 0 must interpret readiness as applying to the particular tick it is considering, not as a generic indication that the mailbox held a command at some earlier point. It must also avoid treating a stale readiness indication as proof that the present contents have been completely published. The proposed publication and tagging rules need to be evaluated together.
Is this plan also a test of incompatible state-migration rejection?

Not as stated. It plans an uncached, tick-tagged cross-core command handoff and a benchmark of core-0 latch latency. Cutover still requires a validated compatible pair, and an incompatible candidate must not be selected. But implementing a mailbox and timing its latch path do not, by themselves, test migration-contract rejection or atomic firmware-state commitment.
Would release/acquire publication make a prepared command recoverable after an update-time reset?

No. Release/acquire publication concerns what the two running cores can observe during an uninterrupted handoff. It does not make a mailbox into a recoverable commit record or establish which compatible firmware-state pair boot will select after a reset. The reset-recovery obligation remains separate from this cross-core publication plan.
How can I keep the description from claiming that ‘uncached’ automatically fixes stale reads?

Call the mailbox and release/acquire rule the *proposed mechanism*, then state what needs verification: core 0 sees a fully published, stable command tagged for the correct tick and validated pair, without delaying the latch beyond its 1 ms deadline. That retains the stale-cache motivation without claiming that a memory attribute alone establishes visibility, freshness, and timing.
Can you give me a concise plan statement with all the specific pieces?

Implement uncached, tick-tagged mailboxes with release/acquire publication for prepared commands. Retain the old firmware’s control ownership until the candidate pair and its required command are ready at a cutover boundary; then benchmark core-0 latch latency against the 1 ms deadline. Verify separately that core 0 consumes the correct published command and that neither duplicated nor skipped actuator commands occur; none of those outcomes is established by the plan alone.

Let's replay the IntegratedCut-512 traces on dual cores with uncached, tick-tagged mailboxes. I want to measure backlog, state equality, stale reads, physical latch intervals, and recovery. How should I frame the run?

Frame it as an integration measurement, not a result: ‘Replay the IntegratedCut-512 traces on dual cores using uncached, tick-tagged mailboxes. Measure the state-replay backlog, compare candidate state at cutover, check whether core 0 consumes stale prepared commands, record physical actuator latch intervals, and examine firmware-state-pair recovery after resets.’ Keep the observations separate. A clear backlog would not prove the mailbox delivered the correct command, and a timely latch would not prove the booted firmware-state pair was compatible.
What does using the IntegratedCut-512 traces tell us about the scope of this activity?

It identifies the trace material being replayed in the dual-core arrangement. It does not make the replay’s outcomes identical to those represented in the traces. The new activity measures how the dual-core mailbox arrangement behaves when subjected to that material. In particular, do not infer a number of new resets, swaps, or successful recoveries solely from ‘512’ in the trace source’s name.
Should core 0 and core 1 have different responsibilities in the replay?

Under the proposed split, core 0 dispatches tick-indexed actuator commands, while core 1 performs migration and prepares candidate work. The uncached, tick-tagged mailbox is the proposed handoff for a prepared command. The replay should keep those roles distinguishable: preparing a command on core 1 is not the same as core 0 consuming it or the actuator physically latching it. The activity does not yet establish that this division avoids interference.
How do I define the backlog measurement without confusing it with commands waiting in the mailbox?

Define backlog as outstanding state-migration or delta-replay work needed to bring candidate state to a specified cutover boundary. Mailbox readiness is a different condition: whether a prepared actuator command for a particular tick is available to core 0. State which work a reported backlog covers and which boundary it refers to; do not count a waiting command as state-replay backlog or assume a ready mailbox means the candidate state has caught up.
If the backlog briefly reaches zero, can I count the candidate as ready to switch?

Not from that observation alone. Clearance must cover all required state changes through the tick defining the proposed cutover. Candidate-state equality must then be checked at that same boundary, and the firmware-state pair and command for the prospective tick must satisfy their separate readiness conditions. A temporary empty-work indication cannot establish all of those properties.
What exactly should the state-equality comparison use as its reference?

Use the state expected at the defined cutover tick after accounting for the relevant changes through that boundary. Compare it with the candidate state that would actually be selected. If the state schemas differ, equality needs a comparison appropriate to their meaning rather than an assumed byte-for-byte match. The activity specifies a state-equality measurement but does not supply a particular schema or comparison algorithm.
Could candidate state match an earlier tick and still pass if core 0 keeps dispatching while the comparison runs?

Not as a cutover-state comparison for a later tick. Ongoing control can generate additional changes. A match at an earlier boundary establishes only an observation about that earlier boundary; if ownership would change later, the candidate must account for the intervening ticks too. Associate each equality finding and backlog reading with the boundary actually examined.
What should ‘stale read’ mean for the uncached, tick-tagged mailbox?

It should mean that core 0 consumes command information that is not the completed, authorized preparation for the tick it is serving—for example, an older command view despite a readiness indication for the intended tick. The test needs to relate what core 1 prepared and published to what core 0 actually consumed. An uncached location is part of the proposed mechanism; its name alone does not establish freshness, completeness, or correct tick ownership.
If core 0 reads the expected tick tag, does that rule out a stale read?

No. The tag may identify the intended tick while the associated command contents are incomplete or left over from another publication. Conversely, fully visible contents can still belong to the wrong tick or candidate pair. The check must cover the relationship among the tag, published contents, validated pair, and command actually consumed, rather than treating a matching tag as the whole result.
Where does release/acquire publication fit in this run?

If the mailbox uses the proposed release/acquire publication, the stale-read check should examine whether core 0 observes completed command contents after the corresponding readiness publication. It should also check that the published view remains the one core 0 consumes. Release/acquire ordering does not itself prevent a later overwrite or prove that the command is authorized for the tagged tick. Those conditions need to hold together in the dual-core replay.
Do I need to look at command values, or would a sequence of tags be enough?

A sequence of tags can show which ticks were named, but it cannot by itself establish that core 0 saw the correct prepared contents. To examine stale reads, distinguish the command view core 1 finished preparing from the view core 0 consumed for that tag. To examine actuator consistency, distinguish both from what was effectively dispatched or latched. The activity does not prescribe a trace format; it requires observations sufficient for the claims being made.
Could core 0 see a current command while the candidate firmware-state pair isn't validated?

Yes, as a conceptual distinction: command visibility does not supply a validation verdict. Cutover remains conditional on a compatible validated pair as well as a ready command. If the pair associated with a visible mailbox command is not the pair eligible for cutover, core 0 must not treat visibility alone as authority to dispatch it as the candidate-owned tick’s command. The replay should make those associations interpretable.
What should the physical latch interval measurement include?

Frame it as a stress-test activity, not a result: ‘Run MailboxDMA-100k on Controller Update v1.0 under saturated DMA. Record physical actuator latch intervals, check whether core 0 consumes fresh tick-tagged mailbox commands, and examine actuator-command continuity across the running update and cutover.’ These are three observations to obtain; the run instruction does not say any of them has passed.

It specifies the load condition under which to examine the mailbox handoff and actuator path. The question is whether the measured behaviors hold under that condition.
