No. MailboxDMA-100k is the activity’s name; the stated activity does not define that suffix as a count of ticks, commands, swaps, or successful observations. Report any exercised count and its unit from the run records rather than treating the name as a result.
Why measure physical latch intervals instead of just core-0 mailbox-read time?

The physical latch interval observes the actuator path at a later point than the mailbox read. A fast read could still be followed by delayed dispatch or latching. Since uninterrupted control has a 1 ms deadline, the physical observation matters; mailbox-read timing alone would be a narrower measurement. Conversely, latch timing would not tell you whether the mailbox data core 0 read was fresh.

Not solely from interval spacing. You also need to associate each latch with its required tick and its deadline: consecutive events can be close together yet displaced relative to tick boundaries. The activity specifically measures physical latch intervals. If you want a per-tick deadline finding, establish the event-to-tick relationship and report that finding separately rather than assuming the intervals prove it.
What would count as a stale mailbox read?

Core 0 would have consumed a command view other than the completed preparation authorized for the tick and firmware-state pair it is serving. A visible tick tag alone is not necessarily enough: the associated contents must also be the published, stable command for that tick. The test should relate what was prepared and published to what core 0 actually consumed; it does not presume a stale read will occur.
Does using an uncached mailbox rule out stale reads by construction?

No. Controller Update v1.0 includes tick-tagged actuator mailboxes, and the proposed publication approach uses uncached access and release/acquire ordering. The test is still needed to examine whether core 0 actually sees a complete, current, authorized command under saturated DMA. Memory attributes alone do not establish tick freshness or prevent a published view from being replaced at the wrong time.
Would a matching tick tag be sufficient for the freshness check?

A matching tag is necessary to identify the intended tick but does not, on its own, show that the command contents correspond to that publication or the selected validated pair. Make the checked event precise: what did core 1 publish for that tick, and what did core 0 consume? The check should not equate finding the right number in a tag with verifying the complete command view.
What does ‘command continuity’ mean in the run?

Examine whether each required tick during uninterrupted operation has its authorized actuator command exactly once, particularly across the tick where the selected firmware-state pair changes. A repeated effective command and an omitted one are different violations. Keep command continuity separate from both mailbox freshness and physical latch intervals: a fresh command may be skipped, and a promptly latched output could still be a duplicate.
Can contiguous tick tags alone demonstrate continuity?

No. Tags could progress while a required command never becomes effective, or two effective commands could occur for one tagged tick. Relate each tag to the command core 0 actually dispatches and to the relevant observed actuator behavior. A tag sequence is useful for checking the boundary, but it is not itself an exactly-once actuator-command result.
If the same actuator value appears in consecutive ticks, should the test flag a duplicate?

Not just because the values match. Two distinct ticks can each legitimately have a command with the same value. The continuity check asks whether each tick’s command obligation was met once, not whether successive values differ. A duplicated command concerns an extra effective submission for one obligation, while an omitted command leaves one obligation unserved.
Should we focus only on the tick when firmware-state ownership changes?

Include that boundary and the immediately following tick, but do not restrict all three measurements to that instant.
